NEWSLETTER · 17 Nov 2026, 07:06

Stromsteuer: Der Ankündigungskanzler will heute liefern

Präsentiert von Die L’Oréal Gruppe Von HANS VON DER BURCHARD Mit PAULINE VON PEZOLD PRÄSENTIERT VON Schicken Sie uns Ihre Tipps hier oder hier | X @vo

Präsentiert von Die L’Oréal Gruppe

Von HANS VON DER BURCHARD

Mit PAULINE VON PEZOLD

PRÄSENTIERT VON

Schicken Sie uns Ihre Tipps hier oder hier | X @vonderburchard @R_Buchsteiner | Das Playbook anhören oder online lesen

Moin Berlin, hier schreibt Hans von der Burchard am Dienstag dieser innen- wie außenpolitisch ereignisreichen Woche.

Ich steige gerade mit Johann Wadephul in den Flieger: Es geht nach Aserbaidschan und Armenien. Donnerstag sind wir zurück: Gerade rechtzeitig für den Gipfel der Koalition der Willigen im Kanzleramt, der noch viel größer wird als bisher bekannt — und von neuen Ukraine-Äußerungen von Donald Trump überschattet wird. Dazu gleich mehr.

Zunächst blicken wir auf den Koalitionsausschuss: Friedrich Merz will heute unbedingt bei der Stromsteuer liefern. Welche Hürden da heute noch drohen und was sonst noch auf der Agenda steht, berichtet Rasmus Buchsteiner. Dazu spricht SPD-Finanzpolitiker Philipp Rottwilm im Playbook Podcast.

Außerdem heute in Ihrem Playbook: Reem Alabali Radovan auf Irak-Reise, Boris Pistorius wartet in Brüssel auf Details zum US-Truppenabzug, Bratwurst-Alarm bei der Union und eine schwere Regierungskrise in den Niederlanden.

**(Anzeige) Eine Nachricht der L’Oréal Gruppe: Für die L’Oréal Gruppe ist Deutschland langfristig ein strategischer Produktionsstandort von globaler Bedeutung. Mehr erfahren**

SEITE EINS

WAS HABT IHR DENN? WIR HABEN ES DOCH (FAST): Merz will Zuversicht versprühen. Der Koalitionsausschuss von Union und SPD werde sich mit der Stromsteuer nur noch sehr kurz beschäftigen müssen, so der Kanzler.

Ach ja: Dass der Deal für die Fünf-Milliarden-Euro-Entlastung stehe, oder zumindest so gut wie, den Eindruck hat Merz schon ein paar Mal erweckt. Und was dann folgte, waren Lieferprobleme. Und gewaltiger Ärger mit der eigenen Fraktion, hinzu kam Druck, Druck, Druck von Hendrik Wüst.

Los geht’s: Am Nachmittag kommen die Union und SPD zu getrennten Vorbesprechungen zusammen. So gegen 17:30 Uhr startet dann die eigentliche Koalitionsrunde.

Hi, ich bin die Neue: Premiere auf SPD-Seite hat diesmal Petra Köpping, sie übernimmt den Platz von Bärbel Bas. Köpping — die Älteren erinnern sich — wollte übrigens selbst mal SPD-Chefin werden, an der Seite eines gewissen Boris Pistorius.

Vorgeschichte: Wenn es stimmt, was der Kanzler in München erzählte, standen der Vizekanzler und er am Wochenende rege im Austausch. Man habe die Zahlen noch einmal abgeglichen.

Recap: Rasmus hat das Comeback des Ankündigungskanzlers gestern bei der CSU in München beobachtet. Hier geht’s zu seiner Analyse.

Wäre schon bemerkenswert, wenn plötzlich geht, was vergangene Woche nicht ging: die notwendigen Milliarden im Haushalt zu finden, um die Stromsteuer-Senkung für alle zu bezahlen. Warum nicht gleich so?

Moment mal: Lars Klingbeil (der gestern in London war) und seine Leute haben des Kanzlers Ankündigungen mit besonderem Interesse verfolgt. Und die Zurückhaltung war groß — was auch Teil des Spiels sein könnte, wie Merz bemerkte.

Klar: Aus der SPD ist zu hören, man wisse um die Stimmung und den Erwartungsdruck in der Unionsfraktion. Und wolle auch eine Einigung, wenn sie dann irgendwie darstellbar sei.

Könnte sein, dass Klingbeil selbst Gegenfinanzierungsvorschläge auf den Tisch legt. Dürfte sich um Dinge handeln, die der Union nicht gefallen — die Abschaffung des Dienstwagenprivilegs zum Beispiel. Oder weitere Kürzungen beim Handwerkerbonus.

„Wir haben eine lange Liste vorgelegt von ineffizienten Subventionen, die man streichen könnte, worüber man auch finanzieren könnte“, sagt der SPD-Abgeordnete Philipp Rottwilm im 200-Sekunden-Interview. Als weitere Beispiele nannte er die Steuerbefreiung bei Kerosin und die Oldtimer-Steuer.

Durchbruch klingt irgendwie anders: „Auch für die Senkung der Stromsteuer wollen wir eine Lösung finden“, hörte Rasmus gestern am frühen Abend aus dem Finanzministerium, dazu die Warnung: „Wir sollten keine finanzpolitischen Experimente eingehen.“

Kannst Du Dir nicht ausdenken: Ganz offenbar kennen sie im Finanzministerium die Vorstellungen des Kanzleramts.

Es geht um: Ein paar liegengebliebene EEG-Milliarden mobilisieren, dazu um einen weiteren Griff in die Asylrücklage, wie Bild berichtet. Finanzpolitische Experimente wohl aus Sicht des Finanzministeriums.

Ach so: Die Stromsteuer wird nicht das einzige Thema im Koalitionsausschuss sein. Sehr wahrscheinlich sogar, dass die SPD ihre Unzufriedenheit mit dem Spritpreisdeckel-Entwurf von Katherina Reiche noch einmal deutlich artikuliert. Es brauche einen Deckel, der funktioniere, um direkt zu Jahresbeginn, nach Ende des Tankrabatts also, für Entlastung zu sorgen.

Sicher: Auch die kalte Progression wird heute wohl im Kanzleramt debattiert.

Pflichtschuldiger Kanzler: Merz weiß, „dass große Teile der Bundestagsfraktion sehr viel Wert darauf legen“. Ob die Ministerpräsidenten genauso viel Wert darauf legen, das alles mitzufinanzieren, ist allerdings eine andere Sache.

Auch auf der Agenda: Die Rente. Da will der Kanzler die Abläufe mit Zeitplänen verbinden. Hintergrund ist, dass es manche in der Union nicht so nice finden, wenn die Kapitalrente von allem anderen abgekoppelt würde.

Die Sorge: Dass es laufen könnte wie beim Bürgergeld aka Neue Grundsicherung. Da gab es (noch mit Bärbel Bas!) ein erstes Reformpaket. Das nächste lässt aber weiter auf sich warten.

Auf Wiedervorlage: Noch einmal soll sich die Koalitionsrunde mit dem Wahlrecht beschäftigen.

Ausgangslage: Die Union pocht darauf, dass künftig wieder alle Wahlkreis-Erstplatzierten automatisch ins Parlament kommen. Die SPD setzt sich für einen Schritt Richtung Parität ein. Wäre langsam Zeit, die Blockade aufzulösen.

Rückblende: Beim letzten Koalitionsausschuss im Oktober ging es so bis gegen zehn. Schweigend zogen erst Markus Söder, dann Klingbeil und etwas später auch Merz von dannen. Kein Statement, keine Pressekonferenz.

Könnte heute anders sein: vorausgesetzt, den Ankündigungen des Ankündigungskanzlers folgt etwas.

KANZLERMAPPE

BESUCH AUS HELSINKI: Vorm Koa-Ausschuss kommt um 9:30 Uhr Alexander Stubb vorbei. Der finnische Präsident hatte sich letztes Jahr den Titel als „Trump-Flüsterer“ erworben, im Oktober versuchten er und Norwegens Premier Jonas Gahr Støre es mit Wladimir Putin.

Das kam nicht gut an: Andere Nordeuropäer und Balten reagierten empört auf das Putin-Telefonat, und auch im Kanzleramt gab es das ein oder andere Augenrollen über die fehlende europäische Koordinierung vor dem Gespräch.

Trotzdem schätzt Merz Stubb sehr: Und mit dessen Kanal nach Moskau, der 1.340 Kilometer langen finnischen Grenze mit Russland sowie der jüngsten Maximalforderung von Putin — Finnland müsse wieder aus der Nato austreten — gibt es ja auch viel zu bereden.

Heute um 15 Uhr dann bekommt Stubb den Walther-Rathenau-Preis verliehen. Die Laudatio hält Joachim Gauck.

DER STUBB-BESUCH IST AUCH EINE VORBEREITUNG FÜR DONNERSTAG: Wie eingangs erwähnt wird der Ukraine-Gipfel der „Koalition der Willigen“ noch größer und wichtiger als zunächst berichtet. 35 Teilnehmer haben bereits für ihre Vor-Ort-Teilnahme zugesagt.

Vom „größten internationalen Event in der Geschichte des Kanzleramts“ ist gar die Rede. Für Merz ein Außenkanzler-Höhepunkt.

Star-Gäste: Die US-Unterhändler Steve Witkoff und Jared Kushner — die direkt zu Trumps Sichtweise nach dem trilateralen Treffen mit Wladimir Putin und Xi Jinping einige Stunden zuvor in Shenzhen briefen können, — sowie natürlich Wolodymyr Selenskyj.

Logistische Herausforderung: Wie organisiert man eine Pressekonferenz mit so vielen Teilnehmern? Merz mus sich wohl auf die E3 plus Selenskyj und Witkoff/Kushner beschränken. Was auch schon eine große Runde wäre …

Anzeige

TRANSATLANTIK

ROAD TO CHINA: Währenddessen beginnt Trump heute seine dreitägige Asienreise. Neben Atomwaffen und dem Krieg gegen den Iran will der US-Präsident am Donnerstag nun doch mit Xi Jinping und Wladimir Putin über die Ukraine sprechen. Das klang am Freitag noch anders in US-Regierungskreisen.

Eigenwillige Bestandsaufnahme: Putin könne in der Ukraine „viel härter“ vorgehen und habe bereits etwas nachgegeben, sagte Trump gestern. Wie genau er das vor dem Hintergrund der zunehmenden russischen Bombardements auf zivile Ziele begründet, bleibt sein Geheimnis.

Erst diese Nacht wieder: Harsche russische Luftangriffe auf Kyjiw; der Verkehr auf zwei Brücken über den Dnipro sei unterbrochen, schreibt Oliver Caroll vom Economist auf X.

Überraschungsgast: Trump hält auch ein Treffen mit Kim Jong Un für möglich. Die Entscheidung darüber, ob Nordkoreas Machthaber nach China kommt, liege aber letztlich bei Xi. Auch Putin wäre laut Kreml zu einem Treffen bereit.

Erster Halt: Manila. Vor dem Gipfel am Donnerstag trifft sich der US-Präsident zunächst mit den ASEAN-Staaten auf den Philippinen, wo sein Besuch im Vorfeld heftige Proteste auslöste. Mit Thailand soll heute ein Handelsabkommen unterzeichnet werden.

DIPLOMATISCHE DEPESCHE

BESUCH IM SÜDKAUKASUS: Heute Mittag trifft Wadephul in Aserbaidschan ein — sein erster Besuch als Außenminister in dem Land, auch wenn er als Abgeordneter schon mal dort war. Als Handelspartner und Energielieferant ist Baku gerade sehr gefragt: Seit Anfang dieses Jahres wird von dort Erdgas nach Deutschland geliefert.

Trotzdem trüben einige Faktoren den Besuch: So regiert Präsident Ilham Alijew das Land seit 23 Jahren mit harter, autoritärer bis diktatorischer Hand. Seit November letzten Jahres sitzt Oppositionsführer Ali Karimli im Gefängnis; vor kurzem begann hinter verschlossenen Türen der Prozess gegen ihn.

Ebenfalls heikel: Der jüngste BND-Skandal, bei dem Ex-Präsident August Hanning heimlich entwendete Geheimdienst-Informationen an Baku weitergegeben haben soll.

Und dann ist da Bergkarabach: In zwei Offensiven in 2020 und 2023 eroberte Aserbaidschan die Region von Armenien. Dort ist man besorgt, dass es noch weiter vorrücken könnte.

Wadephul geht es darum, das letzten Sommer unter Donald Trumps Schirmherrschaft vereinbarte Friedensabkommen abzusichern. „Der Südkaukasus steht an einem Wendepunkt — mit der historischen Chance, Jahrzehnte von Krieg, Gewalt und Vertreibung endgültig zu überwinden“, so der Außenminister vor seinem Abflug.

Stichwort Armenien: Dorthin reist Wadephul morgen. Auch dort merkt man den kalten Atem Moskaus: „Präsident Putin will keine europäische Ordnung souveräner Staaten, in der jedes Land über sein eigenes Schicksal entscheidet“, betont er. „Über eine Annäherung seiner Nachbarn an Europa darf aber nicht in Moskau entschieden werden.“

PAPIERSÄBELZAHNTIGER: Der australische Vorsitz hat gestern seinen Entwurf für einen Abschlusstext zur Klimakonferenz COP31 vorgestellt — und mit dem 18-seitigen Papier einiges an Irritationen ausgelöst.

Auf den Zahn gefühlt: Vor allem Klimadiplomaten aus Europa sind erstaunt über die Forderungen zur Abkehr von fossiler Energie, die der Entwurf enthält. Wie sie das Papier bewerten und weitere Berichterstattung von vor Ort aus Antalya, lesen Sie in unserem Pro Energie und Klima.

JETSET

ZURÜCK ZU DEN WURZELN: Nach dem Abzug von US-Truppen und Bundeswehr reist Alabali Radovan in den Irak, um Berlins weiter bleibende Rolle bei der Wirtschaftskooperation zu betonen. Carlotta Diederich begleitet die Ministerin.

Heimvorteil: Alabali Radovans Eltern stammen aus dem Irak, für sie geht mit der Reise wortwörtlich ein Traum in Erfüllung: „Wenn ich nur noch eine einzige Reise machen dürfte, würde sie mich in den Irak führen. Nach Bagdad“, sagte sie kürzlich.

Sie möchte ihre persönlichen Beziehungen als Brückenbauerin nutzen, sagte sie zu Carlotta — und sorgt mit ihrem guten Arabisch in den Ministerien durchaus für große Augen bei den Irakern. Mit der Reise will sie außerdem Einfluss in der Region sichern — wie schon hier.

Denn: Auch nach dem Sieg über den IS bleibt der Irak fragil. Das Abkommen zwischen Bagdad und der kurdischen Regionalregierung wird kaum umgesetzt, pro-iranische Milizen agieren wie ein Staat im Staate. Seit Beginn des Iran-Kriegs greift Teheran zudem immer wieder die kurdische Autonomieregion im Nordirak mit Raketen und Drohnen an.

Volles Programm: In Bagdad, Mossul und Erbil schaut sich Alabali Radovan an, was deutsche Entwicklungshilfe beim Wiederaufbau eines vom IS verwüsteten Landes bewirkt. Außerdem auf der Agenda: die Wasserkrise. Dem Zweistromland geht zunehmend das Wasser aus. Der Klimawandel verschärft das Problem.

Ganz ohne Mitbringsel kommt die Ministerin nicht: 70 Millionen Euro hat sie für bilaterale Projekte dabei. Die müssen allerdings auch vom Irak mitfinanziert werden. Große Geldgeschenke sind angesichts der angespannten Haushaltslage ohnehin nicht drin.

BENDLERBLOCK

NATO CALLING: Boris Pistorius ist heute und morgen in Brüssel. Im Nato-Hauptquartier treffen sich die Verteidigungsminister zum EU-Rat und zur Ukraine-Kontaktgruppe UDCG. Am Abend beginnt das Schuman Forum, für das Pistorius auch noch morgen in Brüssel bleibt.

Special Guest: Elbridge Colby, US-Unterstaatssekretär und Policy-Chef im Pentagon, der auch am Treffen der EU-Minister teilnehmen wird, wie Rixa Fürsen erfuhr.

Die Europäer wollen von Colby wissen, was Donald Trump mit Xi Jinping und Wladimir Putin am Donnerstag beim APEC-Gipfel besprechen will. Aber auch, wie es mit dem Truppenabzug aus Europa weitergeht. Noch vor Weihnachten soll die US-Force Posture Review kommen; laut letzten Berichten soll der Abzug kleiner ausfallen (nur 5.000 statt 25.000 Soldaten).

Blick nach Osten: Es soll weiter an dem Winterpaket für die Ukraine geschnürt werden. Vor allem geht es um mehr Luftverteidigung.

Dauerbrenner: Ob man Länder wie Griechenland und Spanien bewegen kann, doch noch Patriot-Systeme an die Ukraine abzugeben.

Vom Strategischen ins Praktische: Während in Brüssel über Abschreckung gesprochen wird, übt die Bundeswehr sie in Litauen. Heute beginnt die zweite Übung der Brigade Litauen „Freedom Shield 26-II“ — mit rund 3.800 Soldaten.

EUROVISION

KANN ROB JETTEN SEINEN JOB RETTEN? Nicht meine Zeile, sondern von Thomas Gutschker, an den an dieser Stelle schöne Grüße gehen. Hintergrund ist die seit letzter Woche schwelende Haushalts- und Regierungskrise in den Niederlanden, aufgrund der das in Minderheit regierende Kabinett des Premiers auch weiterhin am seidenen Faden hängt.

Noch bis spät gestern Abend dauerten die Krisengespräche im „Catshuis“ in Den Haag an — und sollen heute weitergehen. Dagegen wirkt so mancher Koalitionskrach bei uns weniger dramatisch. Den EU-Gipfel in Dublin letzte Woche verpasste Jetten bereits; ob er es wohl noch zur Koalition der Willigen am Donnerstag schafft?

FÖRDERALISTISCHER BETRIEBSAUSFLUG: Erstmals treffen sich die Digitalminister von Bund und Ländern in Brüssel. Welche Baustellen die Länder nach Brüssel mitbringen, lesen Sie bei Technologie und KI.

FRAKTIONSEBENE

JETZT GEHT ES UM DIE WURST: Einige Unionspolitiker sorgen sich um eine ab dem ersten Januar geltende Vorschrift im Umsatzsteuergesetz, wonach Städte, Gemeinden und andere öffentliche Einrichtungen in bestimmten Fällen Umsatzsteuer zahlen müssen.

O-Ton: „Uns erreichen derzeit vermehrt Hinweise auf vermeintliche zusätzliche Umsatzsteuerbelastungen von z.B. Bratwürsten ehrenamtlicher Veranstaltungen, insbesondere bei Schulfesten und Veranstaltungen Freiwilliger Feuerwehren“, teilt der finanzpolitische Sprecher der Fraktion, Fritz Güntzler, in diesem Schreiben mit.

Keine Extrawurst nötig: Auf die Forderung, die Übergangsfrist weiter zu verlängern oder die Gesetzeslage sogar nochmal zu ändern, reagiert Güntzler jedoch abwiegelnd.

Entscheidend sei schließlich, „wem die Umsätze steuerrechtlich zuzurechnen sind und ob überhaupt eine nachhaltige unternehmerische Tätigkeit vorliegt“. Der Bratwurstverkauf etwa werde der Feuerwehrkameradschaft, nicht der jeweiligen Kommune zugerechnet.

BAND DES BUNDES

WISSEN, WO ES HAKT: Katherina Reiches Haus will die Halbleiterbranche zum Testfall für staatliches Lieferkettenmonitoring machen. Ein neues „Chips Office“ soll Abhängigkeiten analysieren und ein Frühwarnsystem aufbauen.

Überforderung: Warum sich das Ministerium hierzu Hilfe von einem externen Dienstleister sucht, lesen Sie bei Industrie und Handel.

JOBWECHSEL

FÜHRUNGSWECHSEL: Die Funke-Chefredakteurin Digital Melanie Amann wird ab Januar alleinige Chefredakteurin der Funke Zentralredaktion, gemeinsam mit Stellvertreterin Anne-Christine Merholz. Damit übernimmt sie von Jörg Quoos nach elf Jahren, der künftig als Editor at Large arbeitet.

SPOTTED

SCHLECHTER GESCHMACK: AfD-Bundespräsidentenkandidat Thomas Berthold irritiert mit Verschwörungstheorien und anderen fragwürdigen Thesen — etwa, dass man sein eigenes Urin gegen Unwohlsein und Erkältung trinken solle. Manche begegnen dem mit schwarzem Humor.

ETWAS SCHADE: Immer wieder hat Friedrich Merz begeistert übers Fliegen gesprochen — wegen der Kanzlerschaft fehlte ihm jedoch die Zeit, um die notwendigen Flugstunden für das Beibehalten der Pilotenlizenz zu absolvieren. Auch seinen Privatflieger hat er verkauft; zum CDU-Landesparteitag in Schleswig-Holstein ging es nur als Passagier im Cockpit eines gecharterten Fliegers, berichtet die Bild.

BUHRUFE BEIM STAHLGIPFEL: Die Rede von Katherina Reiche wurde beim Stahlgipfel immer wieder durch Protestaktionen gestört, berichtet Tom Schmidtgen aus Salzgitter. Arbeiter des Stahlwerks buhten zu Beginn und am Ende, zudem hielten sie Schilder der IG Metall mit Forderungen wie „Grüne Leitmärkte jetzt“ und „Fünf Cent jetzt“ nach oben.

Bitte mehr loben: „Ich würde mir wünschen, dass der ein oder andere sagt: Gut gemacht“, so Reiche zur Branche. In Brüssel habe sie etwa einen Industriestrompreis durchgebracht.

Aufmunterung: Den Strompreis von fünf Cent pro Kilowattstunde hält Reiche für möglich. „Wir sind nicht nur nah dran, wir können das erreichen“, sagte sie auf eine Frage von Tom.

AGENDA

— Erziehung im Digitalzeitalter: Um 11 Uhr eröffnet Stefanie Hubig im Kaiserin-Friedrich-Haus eine Tagung zur gewaltfreien Erziehung.

— Hopfen und Malz: Ebenfalls um 11 Uhr besucht Alois Rainer die Klosterbrauerei im brandenburgischen Neuzelle. Eingeladen hat ihn der Deutsche Brauer-Bund.

— KI im Mittelstand: Um 13:30 Uhr spricht Alexander Schweitzer ein Grußwort bei der Jahrestagung der Zukunftszentren im dbb forum. Das Thema: Was KI und Digitalisierung kleinen und mittleren Unternehmen bringen. Anschließend diskutiert er auf dem Podium.

— Bauen, bauen, bauen: Am späten Nachmittag diskutiert Verena Hubertz beim Tag der Wohnungswirtschaft mit Axel Gedaschko, dem Chef des Wohnungsverbands GdW.

— Forschung auf Eis: Noch bis Freitag reist Dorothee Bär mit Wissenschaftlern durch die Antarktis.

— Klimagipfel am Mittelmeer: Ebenfalls bis Freitag läuft im türkischen Antalya die Weltklimakonferenz. Für Deutschland ist Carsten Schneider dabei.

ZU GUTER LETZT

SCHIRMHERRSCHAFT: Der Tag beginnt grau und ab mittags regnet es immer wieder leicht, die Temperaturen bleiben bei bis zu 8 °C.

GRUß AUS DER KÜCHE:

— Mitarbeiterrestaurant JKH: Mediterrane Gemüselasagne mit Paprika, Zucchini, Karotten, Tomaten und Rucola oder Seelachsfilet mit Zitronen-Schnittlauchsoße, Karotten und Dillkartoffeln

— Lampenladen PLH: Bunte Tortellini, dazu Spinat-Sahnesoße und Parmesan oder Schweinesteak mit Schmorzwiebeln, dazu Kohlrabi mit Semmelbrösel und Salzkartoffeln

— Kantine RTG: Griechische Zucchini mit Hackfleisch, Feta und Oliven, dazu Pilawreis und Kräuterdip oder Veggie-Burger mit Kimchi-Patty und Miso-Mayonnaise, dazu Rotkohl und Wedges

-Auto: Elon Musk sieht, was deutsche Autobauer nicht sehen

-Energie: Deutsches Stromnetz bremst Industrie aus

-Bahn: Dubiose Russlandgeschafte von DB Cargo

https://click.redaktion.handelsblatt.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNjMsInQiOjk5NzEsInMiOjd9AAcAAAAACX-bptIEiY_YVPutc1BQl3kqwuObEabo64fwRPe1aRF6wcy8TZj7r3OeGl9Qtj2sKaWkRit_d8peiBJoAmJ3mS3YDo6zh0-s9CK8Vp0

Tesla in Grünheide: Wachstumsobjekt. (Foto: Sebastian Gollnow/dpa)

Guten Morgen, liebe Leserin, lieber Leser,sieht er was, was wir nicht sehen? Elon Musk will eine Milliardenwette auf den Industriestandort Deutschland eingehen. Wahrend Volkswagen Werksschließungen diskutiert und Mercedes einen Investitionsstopp in Deutschland verhangt hat, will der Amerikaner sein Tesla-Werk im brandenburgischen Grünheide für drei Milliarden Euro um eine Werkshalle erweitern.

Warum gelingt Musk, was deutschen Autobauern derzeit nicht gelingt? Zumindest arbeitet Musk unter zwei Bedingungen, die VW, Mercedes und BMW so nicht haben:

- Musk hat durch eine ziemlich harte Erpressungsstrategie die IG Metall im Werk kleingehalten. Die jetzigen Investitionen etwa machte er davon abhangig, dass die Gewerkschaft bei Betriebsratswahlen keine Mehrheit erhalt – was bisher auch gelang. Einen Tarifvertrag gibt es weiter nicht, Tesla-Mitarbeitende arbeiten drei Stunden wochentlich mehr, bei niedrigerem Gehalt. - Musk geht eine Wette ein, die in vielen anderen Unternehmen zu riskant ware. Denn in der neuen Werkshalle will Tesla vor allem sein Robo-Taxi bauen, in der Endstufe bis zu eine Million Stück. Das Problem: Fahrgaste befordert das Modell bislang nur im texanischen Austin, regular zugelassen ist es nicht einmal in den USA. In Europa ließen sich von dem Wagen ohne Lenkrad derzeit hochstens 1500 Stück pro Jahr zulassen. Dass sich das bis 2029 andert, wenn das Werk fertig sein soll, ist kaum absehbar.

2019 kündigte Musk an, ab 2020 würden mehr als eine Million Robo-Taxis auf den Straßen herumfahren. Heute sind es gerade mal einige Hundert. Nicht ausgeschlossen, dass die Prognosen für das Werk in Grünheide ahnlich treffsicher sind. Aber immerhin prognostiziert mal jemand Wachstum und nicht Niedergang.

KI: Woche der Wahrheit startet trist

Anlegerinnen und Anleger schauen skeptisch auf die Woche der Wahrheit für die Künstliche Intelligenz. Die Auswirkungen des Rücktritts von Nvidia-Chef Jensen Huang und die Sorge vor einem Ende des KI-Booms haben die US-Borsen gestern Abend ins Minus gedrückt. Der Index der Technologieborse Nasdaq sackte um 2,5 Prozent auf 24.509 Punkte ab.

Vor allem der Chip-Konzern Nvidia verlor mit 4,1 Prozent deutlich, rutschte bei der Marktkapitalisierung hinter Microsoft. Zuvor hatte das Board des Unternehmens mitgeteilt, der am vergangenen Donnerstag nach Affaren und Spionagevorwürfen zurückgetretene CEO Jensen Huang werde nicht zurückkehren. Heute Abend legt Huangs Interims-Nachfolgerin Colette Kress Quartalszahlen vor – von denen hangt einiges ab für die Stimmung der Borsianer. Ahnlich nervos schauen die Markte auf Anthropic. Das KI-Labor will Ende der Woche an die Borse. Zudem verhangte die Regierung von US-Prasident Donald Trump neue Exportbeschrankungen für hochmoderne KI-Chips nach China.

Immerhin sagte Trump gestern, was einige an den Markten offenbar horen wollen, auch wenn es als unwahrscheinlich gilt: Seinetwegen konne Huang zurückkehren:

Ich denke, er hat eine große Lektion gelernt.

Energie: Stromnetz bremst Industrie

Die Leiden der deutschen Industrie sind vielfaltig, manchmal aber auch einfach banal: So scheitert eine wachsende Zahl an Industrie-Investitionen an einem profanen Stromanschluss. Die Netzbetreiber kommen mit neuen Anschlüssen für Großverbraucher nur derart langsam voran, dass der Bau von Rechenzentren, Lkw-Ladesaulen oder Industrieanlagen zum Teil mehr als ein Jahrzehnt warten muss.

Bürokratie und ein Ausbauboom, mit dem die Netzbetreiber nicht Schritt halten, bremsen die Elektrifizierung der Industrie. EWE-Netz-Chef Torsten Maus sagte meiner Kollegin Catiana Krapp:

Die Stromnetzengpasse werden für den Wirtschaftsstandort Deutschland zum Problem.

Nun hat das Land zuletzt aufgewühlte Debatten darüber geführt, welche Art der Stromerzeugung die zukunftsfahigste sei. Womoglich ware mehr Konzentration darauf, wie der Strom überhaupt zum Verbraucher kommen soll, sinnvoller gewesen.

Lars Feld: Der Offenbarungseid der Union

In Berliner Politikkreisen halt sich die Erzahlung, dass ein eigentlich wirtschafts- und finanzpolitisch serioser Bundeskanzler standig unvernünftige Zugestandnisse machen müsse, um die SPD bei Laune zu halten. Der Freiburger Okonom Lars Feld raumt mit dieser Erzahlung ein wenig auf. Feld hat sich den Haushaltskompromiss von Union und SPD – so er denn über den heute tagenden Koalitionsausschuss Bestand hat – angeschaut. Und kommt zu einem bemerkenswerten Ergebnis.

Ob Fortschreibung der Gastro-Mehrwertsteuer-Ausnahme oder Rücknahme der geplanten Elterngeld-Kürzungen: Die Union hat der SPD nicht nur in vielen Fallen klein beigegeben, sondern selbst auch allerlei Unsinniges auf den Weg gebracht. Feld schreibt:

Liebgewonnene Zuwendungen des Staates geben auch die Bürgerlichen nicht gern auf.

Das allerdings hat fatale Folgen:

Die Eckpunkte und Volumina dieser Haushaltsplanung sind beunruhigend.

Für Feld steht fest:

Diese Einigung ist für CDU/CSU ein Offenbarungseid.

Fünf EU-Staaten prasentierten ihre Plane für Ruanda. (Foto: Helmut Fohringer/APA/dpa)

Migration: Ist Ruanda wirklich die Losung?

Kein Kabinettsmitglied hat seine Ziele bisher so konsequent erreicht wie Innenminister Alexander Dobrindt – die Zahl der Asylantrage ist dramatisch zurückgegangen. Dennoch haben sich die politischen Hoffnungen nicht erfüllt: Die Migrationswende hat keine Wahlerinnen und Wahler von der AfD zurück zur Union gebracht. Nun zündet Dobrindt die zweite Stufe seines Plans. Die rund 240.000 Ausreisepflichtigen in Deutschland sollen das Land auch verlassen.

Doch das ist schwierig: Weil ihre Herkunftslander oft nicht feststellbar sind, manche dieser Lander ihre Landsleute aber auch nicht zurückwollen. Solche Menschen sollen künftig in Return-Hubs außerhalb der EU gebracht werden. Ein erster soll in Ruanda entstehen, als Pilotprojekt von Deutschland und vier weiteren EU-Staaten. Die Dimension: Für Deutschland stehen laut SPD-Innenpolitiker Sebastian Fiedler etwa 40 Platze für 20 Millionen Euro im Raum. Schwieriger als der ruandische Machthaber Paul Kagame scheint ohnehin die SPD für den Plan zu gewinnen zu sein – sie kündigte gestern schonmal Widerstand an.

Güterwaggon der DB Cargo: Geschafte der Deutschen Bahn mit Russland. (Foto: AP, Getty Images [M])

Bahn: Dubiose Geschafte in Russland

Wenn es der Deutschen Bahn an einem nicht mangelt, dann an Problemen. Insofern ist es keine naheliegende Idee, sich ein weiteres zu schaffen. Aber genau das hat die Bahn nach Recherchen meines Kollegen Jan Lutz getan. Die Bahn-Tochter DB Cargo betreibt trotz des Kriegs offenbar nicht nur weiter munter ein Russlandgeschaft mit Umsatzen in dreistelliger Millionenhohe – sie nimmt wohl auch in Kauf, dass Teile der Erlose der russischen Staatsbahn zufließen. Die spielt eine wesentliche Rolle beim Uberfall auf die Ukraine.

https://click.redaktion.handelsblatt.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNjMsInQiOjk5NzEsInMiOjd9AAcAAAAACX-bptIREyx75TL4UjjFhdV5Zj_6e7xc8swrOCGOgm7mWgn3a3ZgoatYwBlMqh0gamINtxZ_bujtmRR3U0yFTB71dDhF-_RYRT5X6N8

Den Recherchen zufolge wickelt DB Cargo ihre Containerzüge zwischen China und Deutschland über die russische Staatsbahn ab. Das Unternehmen beteuert, sich an alle Sanktionen zu halten. Sanktionsexperte Viktor Winkler sagt dagegen: „Mir fehlt bei bestem Willen die Fantasie, wie die DB Cargo die horrenden Sanktionsrisiken hier in den Griff bekommen will.“ Nun ist das In-den-Griff-Bekommen von Problemen nicht die Kernkompetenz der Bahn. Dass sie als bundeseigenes Unternehmen aber besser keine Geschafte mit einem Land macht, das seine Nachbarn offen angreift, sollte sich selbst im Bahn-Tower herumgesprochen haben.

Robert Pattinson: Mit Understatement zum James Bond. (Foto: AP)

Film: Gestatten, Bond

Zum Schluss schauen wir auf eine Lieferung, die deutlich langer gedauert hat, als man es von Amazon gewohnt ist. Mehr als fünf Jahre nach Daniel Craigs letztem Einsatz hat der Konzern, der bei James Bond inzwischen das Sagen hat, einen neuen 007 prasentiert: Robert Pattinson, 40, Brite. Ein Starttermin für den Film steht noch nicht fest, hier bleibt die Sendungsverfolgung also lückenhaft. Die Rolle einen wahr gewordenen Traum zu nennen, sei eine Untertreibung, ließ Pattinson gestern mitteilen. Für einen britischen Geheimagenten ist das ein guter Anfang: Understatement kommt da immer gut.

Ich wünsche Ihnen einen Dienstag, an dem Sie sich das ein oder andere Understatement auch leisten konnen.

Herzliche Grüße

The Era of Permanent Technical Difficulties

Plus: All eyes on Nvidia. Trump’s week in Asia. Is Musk meddling with Ukraine? A rare DEI win. And meet your new James Bond.

Jessica Yellin and Rohan Montgomery

Nov 16

READ IN APP

A passenger looks at flight information displays showing cancellations at LAX. Airlines are struggling to return to normal operations after a major communications outage Friday and an unspecified technical issue with United Airlines today. (Photo by Apu GOMES / AFP via Getty Images)

For daily news, updates, and analysis, be sure to follow us on Instagram. If you are able to support independent journalism, please make a tax-deductible donation to News Not Noise here.

We have entered the era of permanent technical difficulties.

Last week it was Microsoft and the FAA. Today it’s the banks. And now United Airlines. Let’s hope social media is next. (Kidding. Not kidding?)

Perhaps this was inevitable when our lives depend on technology, our infrastructure is decades overdue for an upgrade, and our politics treats keeping things working as sinister acts of big government.

The theory is that last week’s FAA outage involved aging infrastructure overwhelmed by new technology. But there’s another possibility: a cyberattack. So how do we distinguish a hostile act from a government that can’t keep the lights on?

I asked a national security source. The response: “In a sufficiently stupid administration, gross incompetence and an attack are indistinguishable.”

Which makes it reassuring that the next Congress will finally conduct some oversight. Until then, back up your devices.

Here Are Your Headlines

More SNAFUs: Two more massive technical issues struck in quick succession today:

Stuck on the Ground: United Airlines apologized for a technical issue that it said caused a “widespread system outage” impacting departing flights. Though the problem lasted less than an hour before being resolved, it delayed hundreds of flights Monday afternoon. It was reportedly unrelated to the issue that forced the FAA to ground flights nationwide.

Don’t Bank On It: Thousands of people across the country reported problems accessing key banking services. Chase blamed a “technical issue,” not a cyberattack, which apparently caused knock-on effects in the financial system. They assured customers accounts are still secure; the issue is with online banking.

Up In The Air: The effects of the FAA’s rare nationwide ground stop are mostly worked out, but key questions remain about what caused it and how to prevent a repeat. The Trump administration blamed two routers, one in an Arkansas facility that was just upgraded from copper wire to fiber optic cable, and one in a Texas facility that had been upgraded weeks ago; they claim both flooded the FAA’s outdated telecommunications network, causing failures and forcing the agency to shut the whole thing down. Officials aren’t sure why the routers failed. Multiple aviation and national security sources News Not Noise spoke with suspect the rollout of a new AI system and other software upgrades overloaded old infrastructure; they also wouldn’t rule out cyberattacks. See my report here. There are reports that the FBI may have taken possession of the routers. Officials denied that, saying the FBI is merely “assisting” the FAA and L3Harris’ investigations. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy refused to apologize, blaming previous administrations and L3Harris, the contractor responsible for maintaining and upgrading the FAA’s telecommunications network. Not everyone buys it. One expert said the idea a router could “take down a national network is just not plausible.”

Sky-High Request: The administration wants Congress to give the FAA $50 billion, which Duffy claims is necessary to fund an entirely new telecommunications network. He hasn’t broken down where the money would go, and his previous request, for about $30 billion, was mostly intended for improving airport terminals. Democrats noted the FAA has spent less than 10% of the $12.5 billion Congress gave it last year. Duffy claims he can’t use those funds for new telecommunications architecture — but lawmakers specifically earmarked $4.75 billion for “telecommunications infrastructure modernization.” Critics see the request as another way for Team Trump to funnel taxpayer dollars to private companies.

Long Haul: America’s air traffic control communications network is infamously outdated, and modernization is taking far longer than in other countries. The Trump administration accelerated things last year, prompting the nonpartisan Government Accountability Office to warn recently that its plan “could be prioritizing speed over costs and air traffic disruptions.” L3Harris, the contractor that owns and is updating the FAA’s communications system, makes about 75% of its revenue from the federal government, and earns roughly $1 billion a year in profit. Last year it agreed to pay $63 million to settle accusations it lied about prices of contracts with the Pentagon. Shortly before that it was tapped to handle the retrofitting of Trump’s Qatar-gifted Air Force One. The administration wants to pay AT&T, which reportedly donated millions to Trump’s inauguration and ballroom, to build an entirely new network.

Follow the Money: Administration officials insisted there is no evidence that a cyberattack or the FAA’s new AI tool were involved. That tool, called “SMART,” cost $875 million, and was recently rolled out nationwide. The contract went to a startup called ASI, which gave thousands of dollars in campaign donations to Duffy’s son-in-law and is backed by companies like Andreessen Horowitz that have donated millions to Trump-aligned PACs.

Share

Reboot: The Nvidia scandal is dividing Silicon Valley and the Trump administration. The company’s board reportedly ruled out reinstating disgraced founder Jensen Huang, who was said to be discussing a potential comeback with a “war room” of key allies in Silicon Valley. He has widespread support, including from fellow tech titans like Elon Musk, Trump, and more than 186,000 people — including tens of thousands of shareholders and thousands of employees — who signed an open letter calling for his reinstatement. One problem, his allies admit, is rehabilitating his reputation — not to mention the legal liability of extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two work subordinates. Not everyone is on board. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a “dramatic shake-up” in Nvidia’s leadership. He accused the company of using “seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues.”

Chipping Away: Nvidia will report its quarterly earnings tomorrow. Investors are paying close attention to the money coming from sales to China. They’ll also look at sales to Southeast Asia, where companies build data centers with advanced Nvidia chips and sell access to Chinese firms. It’s a major loophole in America’s AI chip restrictions. Commerce closed it today by restricting chip sales to companies in several countries. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick reportedly resisted the move for months; his family firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, has done huge business with data center companies it affects (and holds millions in Nvidia stock). Trump acknowledged that Lutnick delayed blacklisting Megaspeed, the firm suspected of smuggling billions of dollars of advanced Nvidia AI chips to China. But he defended Lutnick, saying he’s trying to keep relations with China on track.

Coincidence? Last year, Nvidia quietly stopped breaking out revenue from Singapore, where Megaspeed is based. In the quarter before the change, more than a fifth of Nvidia’s revenue came from Singapore.

Just Reward: Commerce is expected to name Nvidia as one of more than two dozen AI “national champions.” The program offers faster export approvals and government support, including federal funding, for overseas sales.

Oh, Also: Trump’s Nvidia investments gained millions in value over the past two years.

Upgrade to paid

Jetsetter: Trump heads to the Philippines today for the annual ASEAN summit, where he’s expected to meet with the leaders of India, Japan, and Australia, America’s partners in a group called the Quad. Then Trump will go to China, where he’ll hold a rare trilateral meeting with China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin. (One might theorize that if we are under cyberattack, the timing of this meeting is no coincidence.) Experts don’t expect major deals, but topics could include nuclear disarmament, Iran, and Ukraine. Trump may also meet North Korea’s Kim Jong Un, whom he recently called a “friend.”

Round 2: Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three young children in 2023, will be retried in March on the same first-degree murder charges. Her first trial ended in a mistrial when a single juror held out. (Catch up on that here.) The judge rejected the defense’s motion to dismiss.

More Meddling: Ukraine’s access to Starshield, the military version of SpaceX’s satellite internet service Starlink, is again being restricted, this time in Russian-occupied areas. SpaceX denies it; Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused the Musk-owned company of lying. He warned the restrictions expose the country’s energy infrastructure to Russian attacks as winter approaches, and have “very dangerous” political implications — i.e., “partially recognizing the temporarily occupied territories” as belonging to Russia. Zelenskyy also said U.S. negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff asked if Ukraine would cede the Donbas region to Russia in return for NATO membership or similar security guarantees.

New Approach: New York City is disbanding the NYPD’s Strategic Response Group, a controversial policing unit that dealt with both terrorism and protests, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced. Created in 2015, the unit drew widespread criticism, including from a former official who helped create it, and multiple lawsuits over its aggressive handling of protests. It will be replaced by an unarmed, civilian-led team in the mayor’s office, with no arrest powers, and a “First Amendment Support Team” within the NYPD, trained in de-escalation. Its counterterrorism work will move elsewhere in the NYPD, with no change in cost or staffing. Officers will also face new limits on the weapons and tactics they can use at protests. Mamdani and Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said the changes will “transform” the city’s response to protests, centering “de-escalation and civilian coordination.”

Rare DEI Win: The Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration’s attempt to cancel tens of millions of dollars in DEI-related research grants. That leaves in place an appeals court ruling that the cuts violated the researchers’ First Amendment rights. The Court separately rejected a group of doctors challenging a requirement that their continuing medical education cover “implicit bias.”

Sensitive Topic: The Supreme Court declined to hear a challenge to Maryland’s ban on carrying guns in “sensitive places” like college campuses, hospitals, and bars. Justice Clarence Thomas didn’t dissent but questioned the law’s constitutionality. He suggested a more “appropriate” case could let the Court expand gun rights even further.

Share

Culture, Not Noise

The name’s Pattinson… Robert Pattinson. He’s the next actor to play James Bond. (Photo by Dave Benett/WireImage)

The Bond Community, Shaken and Stirred: Say hello to your new James Bond: Robert Pattinson. The 40-year-old British actor, famous for his roles in Twilight, The Batman, and Tenet, will become the seventh actor to step into one of the most widely coveted (and criticized) shoes in cinema history, succeeding Daniel Craig. He does so at an uncertain time for the franchise, which has gone five years without a new film and is now owned by Amazon MGM. The company last year wrested creative control over the films from the Broccoli family, which had overseen the previous 25 installments. The 26th will be written by “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight and directed by Denis Villeneuve, who said Pattinson “has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new.” Pattinson beat several other contenders, including Nicholas Hoult, Josh O’Connor, and Callum Turner. Not everyone is happy with the choice. But that’s fairly standard for Bond. Daniel Craig, now one of the most celebrated actors to play the role, was widely mocked upon taking the role. Even Sean Connery, the first — and to many die-hard fans the best — Bond faced criticism. Ian Fleming, the creator of James Bond, was “shocked” at the choice of Connery, complaining he wanted “an elegant man, not this roughneck” who “couldn’t speak the Queen’s English.” Let us know what you think about Pattinson as Bond in the comments.

NEWSLETTER · 17 Nov 2026, 00:13

Why the whole world is watching Nvidia

Global power is in flux. Your daily guide to what comes next. By JACK BLANCHARD Welcome to POLITICO Forecast. This is Jack Blanchard, delighted to see

Global power is in flux. Your daily guide to what comes next.

By JACK BLANCHARD

Send tips here | View in your browser

Welcome to POLITICO Forecast. This is Jack Blanchard, delighted to see that 40-something Brits are still not too old to be cast as James Bond. Drop me a line — especially if you’re a Hollywood casting agent with money to burn.

5 THINGS THAT MATTERED TODAY

— Big Tech stocks dived ahead of tomorrow’s Nvidia earnings call and Thursday’s landmark Anthropic IPO, reflecting deep turmoil in the AI industry.

— U.S. President Donald Trump voiced support for ousted Nvidia boss Jensen Huang — but moved to tighten China’s access to the firm’s most advanced chips.

— Spanish election front-runner Alberto Núñez Feijóo told POLITICO he could not commit to NATO spending targets ahead of the Nov. 29 general election.

— President Trump said the war in Ukraine will be up for discussion in his summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin this week, contrary to previous White House claims.

— Ukraine launched its biggest drone attack on Russia since the war began.

THE NEXT NEWS CYCLE

Jensen Huang speaks at a summit in Berlin, Germany on Oct. 19, 2026. | Nadja Wohlleben/Getty Images

HUANG OUT TO DRY: The tech and finance worlds spent the weekend in fevered speculation about where U.S. chip giant Nvidia is headed following the stunning resignation of CEO Jensen Huang. Tomorrow we should get the first hint of what’s coming next.

Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress — the long-serving chief finance officer who stepped up when Huang quit last week — will lead an earnings call with investors and analysts as the firm announces its Q3 financial results.

It’s a big moment, POLITICO Decoded’s Sam Sutton tells Forecast, given the outsized role that Nvidia has played in the global AI industry — not just building its most advanced chips, but using its massive cash pile to invest heavily in AI firms and infrastructure projects.

“Nvidia has been called the Central Bank of AI,” Sam says. “This is a massive company from a financial standpoint. They are highly profitable, they generate a ton of cash, and that has allowed them to be effectively the financial backstop for the entire AI ecosystem. They guarantee commitments for new compute. They support the construction of data centers. And so there’s concern what sort of backstop will be there now that Jensen is no longer at the company.”

“I expect the new CEO will be questioned pretty aggressively on what the trajectory is for the company moving forward, and how it’s going to navigate life without the person who co-founded and led the company for the last 30 years.”

The question marks around Nvidia’s future are especially acute, Sam notes, given the central role Huang has played in setting the firm’s direction since founding it as a small graphics card manufacturer in the 1990s.

“Obviously, Jensen’s personal brand has been completely wrapped up with Nvidia’s, and even as opposed to other high-flying CEOs, he’s viewed as pretty integral to Nvidia’s success,” Sam says. “He founded the business, is intimately familiar with its technology, intimately familiar with its history, and also has been a very effective dealmaker in navigating Nvidia’s relationships with the frontier AI labs as well as Wall Street institutions.”

“He had the ability to take tremendous amounts of risk, and whoever comes next isn’t going to get that same level of deference,” Sam adds. “They’re not going to be able to be as aggressive [with Nvidia’s investments] as he was, and so that raises questions about the company’s future deals.”

That’s part of the reason why Huang’s allies in Silicon Valley spent the weekend plotting an improbable comeback, though it emerged today that Nvidia’s board is determined to move on without him.

Huang’s successor will also have to chart the increasingly fraught issue of exporting chips to China, with questions swirling both within the global AI industry — and indeed within the White House — about the extent to which controls should be applied.

As he departed Washington today for a series of Asian summits, including a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump signalled some support for Huang’s pro-China approach. Trump said he “certainly would not mind” seeing Huang reinstated as CEO, and questioned whether the tech executive he allegedly had an affair with, Alice Huang (no relation), was even a Chinese spy at all.

Crucially, Trump also voiced support for under-fire U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has been blamed by senior colleagues — including U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent — over his department’s alleged lax oversight of Nvidia and China’s access to the company’s advanced chips.

“He’s done a very good job,” Trump said of Lutnick as he defended the Commerce secretary’s failure to crack down harder on Megaspeed, the Singapore company at the center of allegations of Chinese espionage. “If you did do something, you could have a blowup with China,” Trump added. “We’re having a very good relationship with China right now.”

Xi will be keen for that to continue — though Trump added that he could see “both sides” of the debate around tighter export controls and that “you can’t say either is wrong or right.” Even as he did so, his administration moved to tighten one key loophole through which China was believed to be accessing Nvidia’s most advanced chips.

FUTURE INTELLIGENCE

LE CRUNCH: Five French presidential hopefuls went head to head in a TV debate tonight — but the most interesting candidates may not have been on screen at all.

Presidential wannabes including far-right leader Marine Le Pen, far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, conservative Bruno Retailleau and centrist Gabriel Attal duked it out on the TF1 network this evening, POLITICO France’s Clea Caulcutt tells Forecast, with Le Pen in her opponents’ crosshairs for much of the night.

“Tonight was interesting because most of the candidates rounded on the front-runner,” Clea said. “Retailleau and Attal both accused Le Pen of magical thinking on her plans to fix the economy. ‘It’s a joke,’ said Retailleau. Le Pen, who has a commanding lead in most polls, did not rise to the bait — but did spend some time scoffing at Attal, who she accused of worsening French debt levels during his time as French prime minister. “Oh please, no lessons from you,” she shot back witheringly at Attal.

That exchange showed the depth of French centrists’ problems. After a decade with President Emmanuel Macron and his allies at the helm, they are widely blamed for France’s current economic malaise.

And with no standout candidate among an assortment of hopefuls — center-left candidate Raphaël Glucksmann and another former PM, Édouard Philippe, are also in the mix — centrist votes are badly divided, leaving Le Pen and Mélenchon out in front. The question gripping France is whether a new challenger could surge through the middle and take the fight to the far right.

There are still five months still to go until polling day, and a number of colorful characters could yet jump into the race, Clea and POLITICO’s Giorgio Leali reported this morning.

Names being floated include that of Christine Lagarde, the French ex-finance minister who recently announced she was stepping down as head of the European Central Bank so she could speak freely about the elections. “I can no longer stay neutral,” she told reporters in Frankfurt.

Other veteran political heavyweights being watched for possible presidential runs include former Economy Minister Bruno Le Maire; former PM Dominique de Villepin — best remembered for his fervent opposition to the 2003 Iraq War — and even former President François Hollande, who served only one term in the 2010s.

But this is 2026, when political experience and establishment credentials are rarely the best route to voters’ hearts.

Which means the most interesting name currently being thrown into the mix may be that of one of France’s most popular sports stars, the Olympic judo champion Teddy Riner.

A five-time Olympic champion, Riner is a political novice with no party affiliation at all. But that didn’t stop him leaping into the presidential race last week, vowing to put healthcare at the heart of his platform. “France doesn’t need a professional politician who recites talking points and spends all day bickering,” Riner said. “It needs common sense, firmness, justice and a government that sets things right.”

Given the extraordinary success of outsider candidates in global elections over the past decade, from Donald Trump to Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, nobody is ruling him out.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“The relationship has undoubtedly improved on a personal level. There is affability and a certain sympathy.”

— In an interview with POLITICO’s Madrid Playbook, Spanish conservative leader (and likely next Prime Minister) Alberto Núñez Feijóo discusses his increasingly warm relations with far-right leader Santiago Abascal, ahead of an expected post-election coalition.

HARD POWER: THE DEMS’ UNLIKELY INSURGENT

Sen. Chris Van Hollen speaks at the Democrats’ “What’s Next” summit in Denver, Colorado on Nov. 13, 2026. | Mark Makela/Getty Images

Chuck Schumer just steered Democrats to an improbable U.S. Senate majority. But that doesn’t mean he’ll get the chance to bask in his party’s acclaim.

Instead, the Dem Senate leader is scrambling to avoid becoming the latest casualty of the ongoing battle between the Democratic Party establishment and an insurgent left.

Schumer, a veteran New York senator, faces an unexpected leadership challenge from his colleague Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who’s tapping into grassroots frustration with Democratic Party leadership in the Trump era.

Progressives have rallied around Van Hollen and his stark criticism of the party’s old guard — chief among them Schumer, whom Van Hollen has accused of siding “with the crypto industry and [pro-Israel lobbying powerhouse] AIPAC” to block more progressive candidates in Democratic primaries earlier this year.

The 67-year-old Van Hollen makes for an unlikely insurgent. He’s spent decades rising through the Democratic House and Senate establishment, including stints as chairman of the party’s campaign arm in both chambers.

But he’s grown increasingly critical of the U.S.’s relationship with Israel, pushing to restrict arms sales there, and emerged as an outspoken critic of the White House’s hardline immigration agenda. He was the first U.S. lawmaker to visit the El Salvadoran prison where scores of deportees were being held.

That positioning has led many progressives to rally around his challenge to Schumer — who, at 75, is viewed by critics on the left as emblematic of a geriatric establishment that’s out of touch with voters and unable to take the fight to President Trump.

“It’s no secret there is a clamor for change within the party,” says POLITICO’s senior Congress reporter Jordain Carney, “and Schumer has been the focus of a lot of outside-the-building frustration over the past year or so. … Van Hollen supporters believe the size of the majority — including a number of incoming freshmen being anti-Schumer — gives them more momentum.”

Despite Van Hollen’s unexpected role as the Democratic left’s new darling, conventional wisdom still holds that Schumer has enough support within the Senate Democratic Caucus to hang onto his post, Jordain tells Forecast. Schumer has “a decades-built well of support,” she notes, “he helped recruit a number of incoming freshmen — and this is a caucus that is still relatively conflict-adverse.”

“The key for Van Hollen will be how much support he can get outside of those freshmen, and the so-called [left-wing populist] Fight Club, and a couple of well-known Schumer discontents.”

Even after a historic election victory, the Democratic civil war knows no end.

SOFT POWER: EU SPY SCHOOL

It’s been quite a week for spy news, with the Jensen Huang scandal gripping the tech and finance worlds and the white smoke finally appearing in the hunt for a new James Bond.

Now even the dusty bureaucrats of the European Union are getting in on the act, POLITICO’s Antoaneta Roussi and Gerardo Fortuna report, via an EU crash course on honeytraps and other spy-world techniques.

“Officials at both the European Commission and the European Parliament are being put through role-playing exercises designed to show how easily sensitive information can fall into the wrong hands,” Antoaneta and Gerardo reveal. One EU Parliament official told POLITICO he had been specifically warned about honeypot scenarios like the one alleged in the Nvidia case.

And in other materials seen by POLITICO, a 45-minute “Cyber Escape Game” invites teams of up to five officials to take on a “very special mission,” stepping into the shoes of a spy by breaking into a private office to gather as many clues as possible about their target.

A second EU Parliament official who took part in the exercise, told them: “The aim was to make us realize just how much we can find out by combining information we find online with details found in an office or a wastepaper basket.” See you tomorrow.

TUESDAY’S AGENDA

— Nvidia executives hold earnings call with analysts as the firm’s Q3 results are published.

— President Trump attends meetings with allies at the ASEAN summit in Manila, including the signing ceremony for a U.S.-Thailand trade deal.

— EU defense ministers hold a Foreign Affairs Council in Brussels.

Q: What has been your favorite part of your internship at CSIS?

My favorite part of this internship has been having real input into what I have gotten to research. The most interesting thing I am leaving this internship having learned is the degree to which we are treading new ground and pushing the frontiers as energy professionals this year. South Korea widens AI exam cheating probe as fairness concerns grow nationwide

John Lee

South Korea has launched an investigation into 528 national qualification categories administered this year following the confession of a tax accountant examination’s top scorer that he used artificial intelligence (AI) and concealed electronic devices to cheat. Building Visual Intelligence — Andreas Blattmann & Dustin Podell, Black Forest Labs

Black Forest Labs’ case for learning AGI from pixels, motion and sound.

swyx .ai | November 16, 2026

This episode is sponsored by Deepgram. Try Deepgram for voice agents that truly understand your context! #contextiseverything

Why FLUX 3 Trains on Images, Video and Sound — Andreas Blattmann & Dustin Podell, Black Forest Labs

Not many people know that Stable Diffusion is why I went fulltime into AI (I aptly titled Multiverse, not Metaverse to call out Zuck’s mistaken investment). It turns out that Dustin Podell also had the same aha moment - quitting his day job when the model came out. But we took very different paths… I stuck to what I knew in human content creation, and Dustin immersed deep into AI content creation with Andreas Blattmann, co-inventor of Latent Diffusion and the rest of the world-leading imagegen crew at Stability AI. Stability fell apart, but Anj Midha helped the core group spin out to BFL, which immediately built an incredible new imagegen model in the Flux series. But why are they now going into video and world models?

Andreas gives an example you can try with one hand. If somebody tosses you a ball, your hand starts moving before the ball reaches you. You can do that without being able to write down the trajectory. When he talks about building visual intelligence, that’s the kind of knowledge he means. A still can show you where the ball is. A video shows you how it got there. The sound of impact can tell you when it hit something, even if the camera missed the contact. That’s BFL’s argument for training FLUX 3 on the three signals together. BFL’s FLUX 3 release

The horse in motion is one of the FLUX 3 examples we show in the intro. The audio examples are worth playing with the sound on. FLUX 3 Video

What a moving camera teaches you

Suppose the camera starts in front of a person and pans around them. At some point the model owes you the back of their head. Andreas thinks ordinary two-dimensional video contains a great deal of evidence about what objects look like from other angles. That doesn’t settle whether a model “understands physics,” a point we go back and forth on. It does give you a much better test than asking whether one frame looks convincing.

There’s a good engineering example late in the episode. Sharpen each frame of a clip independently and each frame might look terrific. Hit play and the extra detail can shimmer, because the upscaler made a slightly different decision every time. BFL derives its video upscaler from the same FLUX 3 backbone. Temporal consistency matters even when all the user asked for was a higher-resolution file.

What’s worth spending training compute on?

One of the questions I had for them was whether autoregression was taking over image generation. Andreas gives the other side its due. An autoregressive model can learn from all the tokens in a training example at once. On the diffusion side, the team can distill a long sampling process down to a handful of steps. Which advantage matters depends on whether you’re paying to train the model or waiting for an image to finish.

Dustin’s early Kontext experiment is a nice example of how they decide where to invest. He suspected an image model that could draw a dog wearing a hat already knew something about where hats go. He and a colleague collected a small set of photos labeled with relationships. A training run of a few hours got the model to put a logo on a shirt. It was rough, but it was enough to take to the next offsite. The team then spent months on the data and the model. FLUX Kontext examples

My favorite user story comes near the end. People were feeding FLUX old, degraded family photos, restoring them, then showing the pictures to their families. Dustin says he hadn’t predicted that use. After talking about preserving somebody’s identity across edits and across frames, it’s a lovely example of who actually notices if you get it right.

Congress leader Sonia Gandhi in conversation with Pouloumi Chatterjee of HarperCollins. Photo: @YadavAkhilesh

The Modi government may have allowed some foreign guests of the Congress’s Bharat Summit to reach Hyderabad – the party says that around 115 of 315 such speakers received official clearance but were later denied a chance to come – but that doesn’t mean it was done with them. After the event concluded, The Hindu reports, the authorities stopped a youth leader of Germany’s Social Democratic Party at the airport as he prepared to leave India, questioned him about why he attended the Summit and demanded to see his social media posts. Earlier, the newspaper recalls, other delegates, including former Ivory Coast Prime Minister Pascal Affi N’Guessan, were ‘detained’ at immigration, questioned about their reasons for coming to the event; some others also allegedly had their social media handles rummaged through.

It sure looks like the Modi government “is not content with fighting its political opposition” but “wants to prevent the opposition from even engaging in dialogue with the rest of the world”, said Alessio De Giorgi, a member of the Brussels-based European Democratic Party. He claims that he is among those foreign guests of the Bharat Summit whom New Delhi has refused entry into India – a group among which is the Norwegian journalist Helle Lyng – alleging that the Indian mission in Brussels called him over and said his party’s public solidarity with Rahul Gandhi amounted to foreign interference. “I replied that if India truly was the great democracy it claims to be, I was confident my visa would be granted. Needless to say, it never arrived,” De Giorgi wrote on Facebook.

Foreign interference was also invoked by the BJP in Hyderabad against Giacomo Filibeck, an Italian politician with the Party of European Socialists who attended the Summit and endorsed the Congress’s vote chori pitch. A delegation of Telangana BJP leaders visited the Foreigners’ Regional Registration Office and complained against Filibeck, saying his remarks amounted to ‘interference in India’s internal political affairs’. That is grounds enough to warrant Filibeck’s deportation and blacklisting, the saffron party is reported to have impressed upon the FRRO.

TOP OF THE AGENDA

From wizard to vampire, from Batman to 007

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNjIsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB1nSHPSznQjqDplqwCYOxhQEc9nqJrlpuF9bkUoTnEYrEOmr1bXdWUw7L-1mamQJIuF-W253jscCfdiORQosQimhja47hIobu_TpScVEug A new 007 film is expected to go into production in 2027, with a 2028 release date. Credit: Jaap Buitendijk/Amazon MGM Studios

Robert Pattinson has described getting the role of James Bond as "the honour of a lifetime". The 40-year-old British star becomes only the seventh actor to play agent 007 - see his predecessors here https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNjIsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB1nSHPS09Og8QeKq4Jp9I_BbIXbg6DFn4fKdeajIMV136-N3SmND2YvStu9TrrXwE4di9ehkajNwPrCspFGsy6SlK5mLg9laObjl6tdsiA . While some were relatively unknown when cast, Pattinson's career spans two decades. Perhaps best known for playing vampire Edward Cullen in the Twilight films, Pattinson had his first big break as Cedric Diggory in the Harry Potter series and was the latest actor to play the Batman. His "proven track record of box office success", our entertainment reporter notes https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNjIsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB1nSHPS1JtGe4mioMJHCOLJUZT9D-mDt0QGipkDk2bfSqNYtn7nsU7IXJXpB0jW2ZWDolAaBGTaHgvtA-tSoEYvap7r-pi1rSXTq2Wcvmw , likely played in his favour as producers seek to bring the character into a new era and reach new fans.Meet the new Bond https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNjIsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB1nSHPS2PDAJ42jIoX9LTtu2GX5FqtztdVwFmY_bK0Qt1ZX7w-l9nKOBhzYJWN1HdfyfWNoZyWwH4lhRh3R1f8FQrINVlh5lVu6OoB5dfg

Tech CEOs show support for Huang

An open letter calling for the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO of US chipmaker Nvidia has received more than 175,000 signatures - including fellow tech bosses such as SpaceX's Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, of Epic Games. Huang resigned last week following reports of two affairs, one with a woman suspected of spying for China and another allegedly with one of his employees. US President Donald Trump also said he "would certainly not mind" seeing Huang handed back his job.

AT THE SCENE

Butembo, Democratic Republic of Congo

How a doctor survived Ebola

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNjIsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB1nSHPTFHGQqTZqzV0WXxcVSdMy1hi4lGK7XbbCqGtFXNJ7xikBcZY4H69YGuzJEif9m4zJJCM2I8j1Ut43JUUCACQkv4fS4mxtYETsvIA There is no approved vaccine or treatment for the kind of virus linked to the current outbreak. Credit: Braton Serge/BBC

Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga is one of 3,031 people who have survived being sick with Ebola in the current outbreak, which the World Health Organization declared a public health emergency of international concern in May. He is keen to share his story in an effort to help stop the spread of infections devastating his community.

Ruth Alonga, BBC Africa

The first symptoms appeared gradually: a bitter taste in his mouth, headaches and a general feeling of malaise. He contacted the Ebola response team. After an initial consultation and some tests, he returned home, but his condition did not improve. On the fourth day, he began vomiting and had diarrhoea.

This is when he gathered his family members - including his mother - to tell them he had to go to the Ebola treatment centre. "She had started crying, along with my sisters. I told them everything would be alright, that I was a doctor and that I was confident. But they weren't reassured," he says.

Katie Strick

Hello. Russia's super-rich are busy imagining a post-Putin world - we explore what that might look like. See the Prince and Princess of Wales play cricket in India, their first overseas visit in four years. Plus, meet the unlikely candidate running for French president.

TOP OF THE AGENDA

Why Russia's silent billionaires are growing restless

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNjIsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB1R_lcrFgE3QOxUJXMr1Yfsj5r3Cucc4-CmS78WwpoKsc_pruCF-NweHc1ctT9N6wL05-xXpkO34KSChUSZ2ZaW3RAZb-tOLKmQh9Q Putin has kept tycoons in line with a ruthless policy of carrot and stick since Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Credit: Getty

Russian oligarchs have tended to keep their thoughts to themselves since President Vladimir Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. But some members of the country's once-mighty business elite seem to be wondering if, once the president has left office or died, Russia might look more like it did in the 1990s, our reporter Vitaly Shevchenko writes. Back then, the country was an "oligarch republic", with the ultra-rich in charge and pulling strings at the highest level of power. Some of these tycoons are pining after a "return of politics into people's lives" -- less repression, more open speech, and healthier competition between parties and politicians. But once Putin is gone, will the remnants of the current regime let that happen?

🟡🟡🟡 ‘Heroes have flaws’: Sam Altman on Jensen Huang

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said Monday he has “personal strong empathy” for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huan͏‌ ͏‌ ͏‌ ͏‌ ͏‌ ͏‌

November 16, 2026

Read on the web

Sign up for our free email briefings→

Silicon Valley & The World • Exclusive

‘Heroes have flaws’: Sam Altman says he has personal empathy for Jensen Huang

J.D. Capelouto

Kris Tripplaar/Semafor

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said Monday he had “strong empathy” for ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, but declined to weigh in on whether Huang should return to the chip giant.

“Heroes have flaws,” Altman, who had been ousted from his own post in 2023 only to return, said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World convening in California.

Huang is mulling trying to make a comeback as CEO, and some tech leaders are pushing for him to return, but the company’s board is not considering bringing him back at this time, people familiar with the matter tell Semafor.

Asked whether Huang should return, Altman told Semafor’s Reed Albergotti: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.”

Altman said it’s hard to imagine Nvidia without Huang at the helm, but Nvidia is “a behemoth of a company,” and people still trust its guarantee as an investor.

On public sentiment toward AI

In an expansive 30-minute interview, Altman struck an honest tone about the challenges he and the rest of the AI industry are facing, including the Nvidia fallout, the backlash against data centers, and increasing pressures on the cost of capital to fund the AI buildout.

Following the US midterm elections that were broadly seen as a rebuke of AI, Altman said the industry should take a “strong stance” on how it approaches the long-term vision of AI.

He said much of the backlash to data centers is about people latching onto a physical thing to fight back against, but that the real issue stems from people wanting to stay “in control of the future.”

“We should not want to have a ‘handover’ … either gradual or sudden, to AI making decisions about our future,” he said.

The public should understand, he said, that the people building AI are “team human.”

He said he still thinks data centers will get built, but that it’s clear “the engagement with communities is not working for people.” To address those concerns, he said the industry will have to “adapt.”

Altman’s IPO timeline

Some investors have grown concerned with the massive amounts of capital required for the AI infrastructure buildout, and the buildup of debt. With an OpenAI IPO still looming, Altman said he wasn’t concerned.

OpenAI “will go public at some point,” he said, even if there are “real downsides to being public,” including intense volatility.

Altman said he isn’t concerned with there being enough dollars to go around, even if Anthropic is the first to the IPO party later this week.

“That is not a worry,” he said. “There’s been way too much investor demand and not enough supply.”

Around the Horn (28th episode)

If this were an old-school procedural, 28 episodes would put us at season 2. If we consider this exercise to be more akin to a prestige drama from the present-day TV landscape, we might already be on season 5. Let’s go back around the horn.

This is our 28th roundup of articles on China’s AI ecosystem. For new readers, here’s how it works (see ChinAI #376 for the previous edition):

I give short previews of ten articles that caught my eye during a scan through my usual sources (all published within the past week or so). The title for each preview links to the original article in Chinese.

Readers vote on next week’s feature translation by replying to the email and/or commenting on the post with the number of your preferred article. *Extra weight goes to votes from those of you who support ChinAI through a paid subscription.

The main idea is that any of these 10 links would have made for a great feature translation this week — like the The Lowdown tv show’s soundtrack, there are no skips!

1) The final struggles of a batch of near-death robotics companies

Summary: In the last two years, ~30 robotics manufacturers (many of them Chinese) have faced severe operational crises. This piece digs into why some companies are struggling for their last gasps.

Source: 虎嗅 (Huxiu), a well-known platform that shares user-generated content but also publishes their own pieces on China’s science and technology ecosystem.

2) I’m not that optimistic about BAT doing Personal Agents

Summary: As Meta’s Muse and Spear Street Technology’s Instinct have taken off, China’s big tech giants position themselves to develop their own breakthrough Personal Agent. However, this author sees various barriers, with computing power at the top of the list:

Since a personal agent has to remain active, retain context, and execute long-running tasks, it is token-hungry. Given China’s strain on computing resources, “Every unit of compute allocated to a personal agent is one less unit available for other purposes.”

Includes this interesting anecdote: “An insider revealed that last year, when Tencent faced an acute shortage of computing power, it rented a significant number of GPUs from another major tech firm. This year, however, as the scarcity of GPU resources intensified, the other firm was forced to reclaim those units, even paying a penalty to Tencent for the breach of contract.”

Source: 雷峰网 (Leiphone) — media portal that covers China’s science and tech landscape, with a focus on AI-related happenings.

3) For 10 bucks an hour, she sells herself to robots

Summary: In the embodied AI field, demand for first-person perspective (“egocentric”) data has surged. This piece profiles Zhang Li, a sewing machine operator who wears a small camera on her head for an extra 10 bucks an hour.

Source: 虎嗅 (Huxiu), a well-known platform that shares user-generated content but also publishes their own pieces on China’s science and technology ecosystem.

4) Secured a postgraduate admission recommendation by .01 points, reported by roommate the next day

Summary: The baoyan [保研] system, which provides an opportunity to get into graduate school without taking entrance exams, has sparked fierce competition among students. Some even file reports against each other.

Source: 极昼工作室 (Perpetual Light Studio), a reporting unit under Sohu that does longform human-interest stories.

5) DeepSeek lets AI supervise AI, so we tested the super-agent: who supervises the supervisor?

Summary: This piece breaks down DeepSeek’s recent release: a research prototype of a super-agent that manages multiple individual agents and reports back to the human controller. The analysis is more technical than the articles I usually translate.

6) AI Investment’s big issue: not a bursting bubble, but the three-year hardware bull market has ended

Summary: A hedge fund manager’s view on the AI hardware market, which he sees as unsustainable. The trillions already invested in computing infrastructure would require such an increase in demand for services that might not be there.

Source: 晚点 (LatePost) — publishes in-depth analysis on China’s tech scene, known for deeply-sourced reports.

7) The AI bloodbath in short-form dramas: a winter without obituaries

Summary: This August, AI-generated content accounted for 70 percent of China’s top 100 trending short dramas on Douyin’s list. This report interviews people who lost their jobs amidst the rise of AI short dramas.

Source: 脑极体 (Naojiti), a tech media platform based in Tianjin.

8) Shocking! An “Made in India” AI model has been exposed as a Qwen 3.5 wrapper: AI forced to claim it “comes from India.”

Summary: An interesting story at the intersection of sovereign AI, indigenous innovation, and India-China relations. An Indian company promoted their model as “Made in India,” only to spark controversy over its dependence on Qwen 3.5.

Source: China Software Developer Network (CSDN) — the largest software developer community in China, which provides IT news coverage and hosts code

9) Programmers are leaving office buildings for factory floors

Summary: Computer science used to always top the list of most popular majors, but now electrical engineering has risen in priority. The writer talks with programmers who are switching careers as the job market undergoes a structural shift in response to AI.

Source: 极昼工作室 (Perpetual Light Studio), a reporting unit under Sohu that does longform human-interest stories.

10) This major has undergone a brutal collapse

Summary: This has been a bad year for Chinese computer science graduates, facing perhaps the toughest job market in a decade. Obviously, AI is a factor. This piece explores other interesting factors, including how universities over-expanded CS programs, and parents pushed their kids to attend lower-tier universities just so they could secure a computer science major.

If there’s interest in this theme shared by #9 and #10, we can make it a double feature.

Source: 九边 (WeChat public account which I’m not familiar with; came across this because it was recommended by Huxiu).

Thank you for reading and engaging.

16 November, 2026

Lily Jamali

North America tech correspondent

Greetings from Santa Clara, California - home to Nvidia headquarters, where we are monitoring the company's next steps as it prepares to report earnings for the first time since ex-CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week. After admitting that he had been unfaithful to his wife, Huang initially seemed poised to stay, even after it emerged that US intelligence believed he'd had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNjIsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB1fq6N8x_kikzVjdtFgCsp4rYvlLTNNOvlCKkXYXF1tUurEl-yDBvTFPjre7H38Rwnu3uw2vmnFZ7RlTMW4LurF98c6eoFdrJxHdU-Te . He then stepped down after reports that he'd had another alleged relationship with an employee. Now, there's a push to bring him back.

Are you eagerly anticipating the release of Grand Theft Auto 6? My colleague Laura Cress spoke to insiders - including GTA's original creators - ahead of the big day on Thursday. And after the major global Microsoft outage last week, she also asks if we've become too reliant on big tech.

THE DOWNLOAD

What it would take for Jensen Huang to return

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNjIsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB1fq6N8yixBw8lV8fLPSDQ8q-sZgIt0kETAJfdliofTuIsKcBrz-A6zOnATOOA9shiV8siQaePPx7l8N3iBE2VEdAct-qjtUBttaxbdu Nvidia lost billions of dollars from its stock market value last week. Credit: Reuters

The atmosphere at Nvidia's headquarters last week was sombre in the aftermath of Huang's resignation from the company he led for 33 years. Some locals stopped by to drop off flowers and other mementos. It was as if they were in mourning.

"It is the end of an era," a fan named Jason told me. Huang's remarkable rise to the top of the industry led to him being dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech", and he was courted by leaders in both the US and China - read my colleagues' analysis of his rise and fall here https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNjIsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB1fq6N8z5ytfV2MOEEW041yx9DREc9ufC0u8jhwM_K1D3YP4Rp3UirX0Cy9D7omB9JLIQJGoOfkCxSYODnkl77Rw64G8QHc9Q8lRmUzB Sympathy towards Huang culminated in a petition to reinstate him as CEO being signed by hundreds of thousands https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNjIsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB1fq6N80Slo_Mk30AF9iqJqx-2_IZhswCzO2QsuP3Mp4ue4Mp3hCyQxTBX-sXWL1ItHNRArp6KppG_rBzCiQoITW2QzaJC6HxMLrXpqq this weekend, and messages of support from Elon Musk and other tech bosses. A Huang comeback might seem far-fetched to those outside of Silicon Valley. But inside the bubble, many people I've been speaking to are convinced it could happen - despite his personal scandal. A representative for Huang declined to comment on whether he was plotting a return.

In recent years, Huang kept stakeholders happy - as well as leaders of AI companies, thanks to Nvidia's prolific investments. But questions remain about the possibility that Nvidia's chips may have ended up in China in violation of US export rules.

On Sunday, Congressman John Moolenaar revealed that Huang had agreed to testify before three committees devoted to national security. When that will happen is yet to be finalised, and it is expected to take place behind closed doors.

The download: _Whether or not Huang's testimony yields clarity on the events that brought an end to his leadership of Nvidia, a comeback would require a tremendous break with corporate norms._
