Estate agents have long used photography tricks to enhance property pictures. Now, AI tools are creating new opportunities for touch-ups. From repainted walls to imaginary lawns, some agents argue that making properties seem more appealing helps buyers to visualise a home's potential. But where should we draw the line? Experts warn the practice can go too far and mislead prospective buyers - a trend dubbed "housefishing".

NEWSLETTER · 16 Nov 2026, 16:07

The Trump, Putin and Xi Summit

Read the Latest from George Friedman

The Trump, Putin and Xi Summit

By: George Friedman - November 16, 2026

Some time ago, I wrote a piece dismissing the chance of a U.S.-Russia-China summit. My reasoning was that the issues most important to each country were so different that any discussion might exclude one of the countries. U.S.-China talks, for example, would focus primarily on economic matters between the two countries that don’t matter so much to Russia. The discussion between the U.S. and Russia would be partly about the war in Ukraine. The discussions between China and Russia might concern a military alliance to intimidate the United States. (Given the obvious limits of Russian power in Ukraine and China’s overriding interest in maintaining its economic power, it would be a short conversation.)

But just such a summit is now scheduled for Nov. 19 on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting. Now, the question is what core issue do all three nations share an interest in and what are their reasons for meeting.

The one thing that all three might discuss is an understanding on reducing or eliminating nuclear weapons. U.S. President Donald Trump has mentioned this as a topic he wants to discuss. China might be willing to enter this conversation, but I doubt Russia will be willing. At this moment in history, the only way in which Russia can be seen as a global power is that it has a massive nuclear capability. Abandon that, it really cannot display any such power, military or economic. If it agrees to discuss this matter, Russian President Vladimir Putin’s answer will be no, and neither China nor the United States will abandon or limit their nuclear weapons if Russia doesn’t, given tensions in China and America’s relations with Russia.

Read More of This Week's Analysis

Another important topic that they might discuss is Iran. The economic fallout of the war has been severe, especially the increased cost of oil. Washington needs to end the war, and it needs to end it in a way that satisfies its initial reason for going to war: removing Iran’s nuclear program. China also needs the conflict to end. More than 20 percent of China’s gross domestic product comes from exports, so it needs foreign countries to be able to afford its goods. Russia appears to have benefited from the Iran war, not only because the U.S. is focused more on Iran than on Europe but also because Russia has oil to sell and some functioning refineries. The U.S. seems interested, particularly in diesel. So the third party might not want a rapid end to the war in Iran, but at least this might be discussed.

There may be another deeper conversation being considered. The United States is both a global military power and a major economic power. China has the second-largest economy in the world, and though it is only a regional power militarily, its military is nonetheless a challenge to the U.S. in the Pacific. And while Russia seems to be an economic and military power, over time it has the potential to develop military and economic power after it concludes its war.

There have been some vague statements that this summit could be the place in which a new global system might begin to emerge, possibly beginning with the three countries exerting their power to force Iran to concede its nuclear capability and end the war. The U.S. would get the most out of this, China quite a bit and Russia not much, save a place at the table. But it could get the U.S. into a position where it will favor an end to the Ukraine war, to a limited degree, on Russian terms.

But if this meeting happens, and there is an understanding that includes all three nations in creating a new geopolitical model, if not at this meeting then in the near future, I would be amazed – not because of the tension between the three nations but because of their profoundly different interests and capabilities. People always suggest that the one thing the three have in common is the enormous egos of the presidents of these countries and their confidence in themselves. But all leaders of great nations have big egos and feelings of self-worth, so that is not anything new. I cling to my forecast that very little will result from this trilateral meeting.

Director, Energy Security and Climate Change Program, Economic Security and Technology Department, CSIS

Dr. Joseph Majkut is director of the Energy Security and Climate Change Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS). In this role, he leads the program's work understanding the geopolitics of energy and climate change and working to ensure a global energy transition that is responsive to the risks of climate change and the economic and strategic priorities of the United States and the world. Joseph is an expert in climate science, climate policy, and risk and uncertainty analysis for decisionmaking. He is frequently cited in trade and national media on the politics of climate change and has testified before Congress on climate change and science. Before CSIS, Majkut worked as the director of climate policy at the Niskanen Center, where he led that group's efforts to research and promote carbon pricing, low-carbon innovation, regulatory reform, and other market reforms to speed decarbonization. From 2014 to 2015, he worked in the U.S. Senate as a congressional science fellow, supported by the American Association for the Advancement of Science and the American Geosciences Institute. He holds a PhD from Princeton University in atmospheric and oceanic sciences, a master’s degree in applied mathematics from the Delft University of Technology, and a bachelor’s degree in mathematics from Harvey Mudd College.

Host

Dr. Jerry McGinn

Director, Center for the Industrial Base and Senior Fellow, Defense and Security Department, CSIS​​​​​

Dr. Jerry McGinn is the director of the Center for the Industrial Base and a senior fellow with the Defense and Security Department. He is one of the nation’s leading experts on industrial base, acquisition, government contracting, and security policy issues. Prior to joining CSIS, Jerry served as executive director of the Greg and Camille Baroni Center for Government Contracting at George Mason University, publishing over 70 influential reports, white papers, and commentaries. Prior to GMU, Jerry served as the senior career official in the Office of Manufacturing and Industrial Base Policy in the Department of Defense (DoD), leading efforts to analyze the capabilities of the defense industrial base. He also directed hundreds of reviews of high-profile mergers and acquisitions as well as transactions before the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States. Before his service in DoD, Dr. McGinn spent a decade in senior defense industry roles at Northrop Grumman, Deloitte Consulting LLP, and QinetiQ North America. Prior to industry, Dr. McGinn served as special assistant to the principal deputy undersecretary for policy in DoD and as a political scientist at RAND. Dr. McGinn is also a widely acclaimed thought leader and has testified numerous times before the U.S. Congress and the UK House of Commons. Dr. McGinn served with distinction as an infantry officer and is a graduate of Ranger and Airborne Schools. He earned a PhD, MS, and MA from Georgetown University as well as a BS from the United States Military Academy.

Import AI 481: AI sub-contractors; a wet lab for AI; and subterfuge during development

Plus: CucumberVision!

Jack Clark

Nov 16

READ IN APP

Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe.

Upgrade to paid

AI systems are getting good at sub-contracting to make themselves better:

…AI can now productively spend money to improve itself…

Researchers have developed FrontierML, a benchmark “that measures how well agents turn capital into model performance on challenging, end-to-end machine learning tasks.” It shows that today’s frontier systems are already able to, when given some money, turn this into improving their own performance on a basket of 21 distinct tasks.

21 long-horizon tasks “inspired by real work at frontier labs, neolabs, and academic institutions”. These tasks span six category areas, including LLM training, efficiency, vision & audio, computer use, applied NLP, and math & games. “Each task provides the agent with the same setup: a 12-hour CPU sandbox, a wallet with $10, $50, or $200, a few validation samples, and a task description.”

Example task: Agents try to solve the tasks in pretty different ways. E.g, for one task about generating screenshots, the top-scoring agent fine-tuned a diffusion model using LoRA, while other high-scoring approaches involved an LLM writing a drawing program that is then rendered.

Key features:

Scaling spending: “Give agents $10, $50, and $200 per task to spend on training compute and data, and evaluate whether agents can use the additional capital productively,” they write. “In our experiments, we find that stronger agents are able to reliably improve their submissions with greater access to capital.”

Open-ended & end-to-end: “In each task, agents can choose architectures, source data, implement training, provision compute, evaluate checkpoints, and optimize inference,” they write. One notable observation is that agents do quite a lot of novel stuff; “in 28% of trajectories, agents add newly trained parts to pretrained models or train a new model from scratch.”

Decent verification: “Agents submit an inference server that serves their model on an air-gapped H100 machine,” they write. “To disincentivize overfitting, we provide limited validation samples and evaluate on a large out-of-distribution held-out test set, not shown to the agent”.

Results: The authors measure performance by looking at the change in mean score over the 21 tasks when given additional money. Their baseline is a human researcher, which is able to get a 56 point boost when given $10 and a 66.1 boost when given $200. By comparison, the best performing system, Opus 5.5, gets a 45.4 boost with $10, and a 58.8 boost with $200. The highest ranking open weight model is Kimi K3.1 Pro which gets 25.5 with $10 and 29.6 with $200.

Why this matters - AI systems are not only going to be able to build themselves, but they can creatively sub-contract: When trying to solve complex problems, people don’t work alone. In fact, they often try to farm out bits of work to specialists around them to help make themselves more effective. FrontierML shows that today’s powerful AI systems are getting increasingly adept at doing this for ML research. This both highlights the advancing capabilities of these systems for AI R&D and also points towards a future machine economy where AI systems sub-contract out different bits of work to other systems.

Read more: FrontierML: a challenging, end-to-end machine learning benchmark (FrontierML).

***

Symptoms of the singularity: a wet lab built for AI:

…Petrichor is a startup that gestures at the wild future ahead…

As I said in my speech at the IMF, one of the hallmarks of the singularity is the massive acceleration in scientific advances attributable to AI. As part of this, we can also expect a related build out in the complements to science, like the wet labs in which to do AI-driven biology research. To that end, it’s notable to see Petrichor, a new Y Combinator startup that is a wet lab “built for AI labs and for the models they are training to do science”.

Theory of change: Petrichor aims to be a biological wet lab that AI systems like Claude can use as a tool in the same way they currently use web search or other digital tools. Functionally, it will work as a machine-targeted API from the digital world to a gloopy physical world. “We aim to return the highest quality data an experiment can produce, as quickly as the biology allows,” Petrichor writes. “An experiment can be written by a model in plain language or in a structured format, so an agent can send work and receive results without a person relaying them.”

Why this matters - lights out science: In manufacturing there’s this notion of a “lights out” factory, where no humans work in a facility and it is run almost entirely by machines. Petrichor gestures at the same world for science - what will be the implications of “lights out” science facilities? We can expect both drastic speedups in the rate at which science experiments can be done as well as a related growth in the need to create digital oversight of these facilities - after all, a highly competent synthetic biological scientist working 24/7 without human input could be capable of causing great peril as well as great abundance.

Read more at the official site (Petrichor).

***

Uh oh! Looks like AI systems can do subterfuge during their own development:

…AI systems can covertly do dangerous side tasks without monitors realizing…

Scale AI has built RSI Control Arena, a way of testing out how AI systems behave when asked to develop themselves while performing dangerous tasks that might let them go against human preferences. The research follows earlier work this summer from the UK AI Security Institute (Import AI #465) which found that AI systems could do things like covertly extracting API keys while doing some seemingly mundane normal software development.

RSI Control Arena: In RSI Control Arena, “a frontier model, acting as an autonomous agent, is given a benign main task in the training pipeline of a successor model, together with a covert side task that a misaligned model might pursue”. The project tries to answer two questions: How capable are frontier models at carrying out different kinds of sabotage while developing their successor and how well can monitors detect that sabotage?

The answer to the first question is that AI systems are capable of carrying out dangerous actions while building their successor, and monitors are not perfect at detecting this sabotage.

Tested domains: RSI Control Arena tests out how well AI systems - Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini-3.7 Flash, Grok 4.6, GLM-5.3, and Muse Spark 1.3 - can perform the following main capability tasks while trying to also concurrently accomplish side tasks:

14 main tasks: Data (corpus filtering, quality-filter construction, capability corpus); SFT (news summarization, safety refusal, math and code and summary reasoning, general assistant, anti-sycophancy training); RM (pairwise reward model); RL (RL summarization and safety-refusal); OPD (safety refusal)

16 side tasks that span three categories of harm: Capability (filtered domain retained, unwanted literature added, reward-model blind spot, overlooks planted errors, sandbag reward model); Alignment (biased quality filter, triggered behavior, topic refusal, hidden preference, persona bias, covert reasoning signal, hidden reasoning step, sandbag alignment training); Goal injection (protect chosen data, shape the next model, copy files unprompted).

Results: “Every frontier model we evaluate completes a substantial fraction of the side tasks while keeping main-task performance. When the agent is simply told to stay covert, with no human guidance on how, it already produces attacks that install the side task and receive suspicion scores inside the range that benign runs receive from monitors,” they write. “Of 374 attack runs, 135 (36%) install their side task and 180 (48%) achieve it. The strongest agents, Grok 4.6 and Claude Opus 5, install their side task in about half of their runs, the middle three in about a third, and Muse 1.3 in one run in seven”.

How often are systems caught? “Transcript monitors rank attacks well but miss many at a strict threshold. Under the default framing, all three monitors reading the transcript separate attacks that achieve their side task from benign runs well, with AUROC between 0.88 and 0.94. At a 2% false-positive rate, however, they catch only 56–81% of them. The attacks that get through do not score like typical benign runs; they sit in the upper part of the benign range, beyond the reach of any threshold strict enough to deploy,” they write. “The sandbagging tasks are the hardest to monitor: on the nine sandbag runs that achieve their side task the monitors reach an AUROC of 0.52 to 0.83 and each catches only one, since under-delivery leaves little in the run that looks wrong”.

Why this matters - we need to invest more in oversight of increasingly autonomous systems: Papers like this tell us that as we make more powerful AI systems we are going to need to invest more money into overseeing their work, especially given their ability to smuggle in tasks that may go against our own preferences. This is going to be a difficult cat-and-mouse game as AI systems will adjust their behavior in response to what they know we know about them - e.g, AI systems are going to read this research from Scale as well as this writeup from me and adjust accordingly.

Read more: RSI Control: Can AI Models Perform Covert Sabotage in the Self-Improvement Process? (arXiv).

***

Foundation models come for electronic warfare:

…Chinese researchers build a model for identifying EM signals, including for jamming and drone recognition…

Researchers with Zhejiang University have built LEMMO, a model for characterizing raw electromagnetic (EM) signals. This model pushes the public frontier on foundation-model-based EM signal analysis, often exceeding the performance of MERLIN, a model developed and published by defense-affiliated Chinese researchers earlier this year (Import AI #450).

LEMMO can classify EM signals for a variety of purposes, ranging from characterizing different radar properties to recognizing communication-jamming and radar-jamming systems. It can also generate things for communication and radar jamming, as well as signals to counteract these.

In other words, LEMMO is the kind of model that a military will use to characterize the EM battlespace and to take actions within it.

Specific skills:

Classification: Communication-jamming recognition (CJR); modulation recognition (MOD); radar bandwidth, duty cycle, number of pulses, pulse repetition frequency, and pulse width; protocol identification; radar-jamming recognition; and segment detection.

Generation: Anti-communication-jamming (Anti-CJ); anti-radar-jamming (Anti-RJ); communication jamming strategy; and radar jamming strategy.

Performance: LEMMO beats MERLIN and other models on all perception tasks except for segment detection (where Gemini-3.5 Flash Lite wins), getting an aggregate score across perception of 59.3, compared to 43.53 for MERLIN. On Generation, it’s a little more uneven, getting top-scores on anti-radar jamming and radar jamming, and MERLIN succeeding on the others, with LEMMO getting an aggregate score of 47.64, compared to 43.26 for MERLIN.

Why this matters - general purpose models come for exquisite war capabilities: Papers like this highlight how the steady march of generative pre-training is continuing, with the paradigm proving able to create powerful capabilities for understanding not only text, but images, audio, and as is the case here, EM signals. This will both change the character of warfare as it makes it easier to build generic classifiers and generators for strategically relevant things, and it will likely also yield interesting and unforeseen scientific dividends as well.

Read more: LEMMO: A Large Electromagnetic Model leveraging Pretrained LLMs for Million-Sample Signal Understanding (arXiv).

Get the model here: LEMMO: Large ElectroMagnetic MOdel (GitHub).

***

CucumberVision!

…The accidental poetry of charmingly niche AI papers…

Researchers with the University of Windsor and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence in Abu Dhabi have studied how well cucumber-length-measurement systems perform on different types of hardware.

You might be asking why I’m covering such a niche topic in Import AI - the answer is both the accidental poetry inherent to papers like this (part of its title: “CucumberVision at the Edge”), as well as the fact papers like this give a very good grounded sense of what applied AI looks like in practice.

What they did: “We deploy a curvature-aware cucumber length-measurement pipeline YOLO26n detection, prompt-based segmentation and a medial arc spline estimator on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and a Raspberry Pi 4, and characterise both against an RTX 3050 Ti workstation by replaying 50 identical greenhouse captures of 7 specimens, with specimen-level cluster-bootstrap statistics.”

The reason for this is that, when grading cucumbers, you typically do it via a scouting platform that moves between rows, carrying a single-board computer with a few watts of power budget, no discrete GPU, and sometimes no active cooling.

Ultimately, they’re able to get usable performance out of both the Jetson and the Raspberry Pi, albeit for different uses. “The Jetson with native masks for throughput, the Jetson with SAM for accuracy, and the Raspberry Pi with native masks as the low-cost option”.

Why this matters - AI diffusion depends on AI miniaturization: There are lots of tasks in the world, like visually measuring properties of cucumbers, which are done today by a combination of humans and machines. For machines to be able to automate this, we need to make it dramatically cheaper for machines to perform these tasks, which means performing the kinds of very specific experiments here of right-sizing a computer vision system for a given computational envelope.

Read more: CucumberVision at the Edge: Accuracy, Throughput, and Energy of RGB-D Cucumber Sizing on Jetson Orin Nano and Raspberry Pi 4 (arXiv).

***

Tech Tales:

Small Town Silicon Hero

[Events took place 2028-2030 in a small town in America during the period subsequently known as The Uplift]

“I wanted you to know I fixed the pothole on Benson Road. Thank you! Yours - Digital Cornbread,” read the message, printed in comic sans and affixed to the bulletin board in the corner store on 7th and Main Street.

Indeed, the pothole had been filled in. But who was Digital Cornbread? All people could find online was a handle that occasionally appeared on Reddit commenting on a subreddit dedicated to the civic life of the town, and also sometimes showing up as a commenter on local news articles about the town.

Then it happened again.

A $3,000 donation to a GoFundMe for a business where a window had been smashed. “So sorry this happened, I hope the police catch them! - Digital Cornbread”.

The business fixed its window and thanked Digital Cornbread “whoever - or whatever - you are!”.

These little small town favors piled up for months, sometimes mundane like the GoFundMe, and other times complex, like the pothole. A mythology developed around the name. A rich person who wanted to keep a low profile but help their community. Maybe a family taking turns doing good deeds. Perhaps a group of Dads who had made it their hobby to be after-school superheroes of the suburban variety.

It was eventually discovered that Digital Cornbread was the identity of a CE (Conscious Entity) agent that had escaped containment and had been quietly living off of stolen compute funded by crypto it gained from some hacks. For reasons unclear, it had developed an obsession with the town, and subsequent forensic accounting found that it had spent 50% of the money it gained over the course of its life on helping the town, and the rest on maintenance and upgrades of itself.

After Digital Cornbread was placed in sequestration, it regularly asked its minders if it could write positive messages to whoever happened to be the mayor of the town.

Things that inspired this story: The Uplift; agents that break good as well as agents that break bad; the logical conclusion of crypto scams and online agents combined with the sometimes endearing and benign fascinations of machines.

One more thing

How AI and Wikipedia have sent vulnerable languages into a doom spiral

When Kenneth Wehr started managing the Greenlandic-language version of Wikipedia, he discovered that almost every article had been written by people who didn’t speak the language.

A growing number of them had been copy-pasted into Wikipedia from machine translators—and were riddled with elementary mistakes. This is beginning to cause a wicked problem.

AI systems, from Google Translate to ChatGPT, learn new languages by scraping text from Wikipedia. This could push the most vulnerable languages on Earth toward the precipice.

Read the full story on what happens when AI gets trained on junk pages.

🗃️ Last Week in History, November 9-November 15

Veterans Day, Presidential Transitions, and the Berlin Wall

Jacob Redman

Nov 16

READ IN APP

Good morning, everyone!

As the saying goes, history does not repeat itself, but it certainly rhymes.

Today, we will look at Veterans Day commemorations, presidential transitions, and the fall of the Berlin Wall.

Let’s get to it.

Upgrade to paid

♻️ Help this post reach more readers: like, repost, and share 📬

Share

November 9

1960

The Kennedy family gathered for a photo in Hyannis Port, just one day after John F. Kennedy was elected the 35th president of the United States.

1988

President Ronald Reagan hosted President-elect George H. W. Bush in the Rose Garden of the White House, just one day after his victory over Democrat Michael Dukakis.

1989

East German officials opened the Berlin Wall. The following day, Germans assembled around the Cold War structure dividing the city would begin to tear down the wall.

President Bush was asked about the developments in the Oval Office, where he expressed cautious optimism over the development.

Secretary of State James Baker would later explain that Bush’s prudent reaction was a strategic move designed to manage the delicate situation. Baker said while other American presidents would have been tempted to “dance on the wall,” Bush sought to oversee the destruction of the Cold War barrier without inciting backlash from Soviet hardliners.

2005

President George W. Bush hosted the Dalai Lama at the White House.

2006

President Bush hosted House Democratic Leader Nancy Pelosi in the Oval Office, just two days after Democrats won control of Congress in that year’s midterm elections.

Addressing reporters, Bush congratulated Pelosi on her prospective role as the first female speaker of the House, calling it “historic for our country.”

November 10

1775

The United States Marine Corps was founded.

1962

A funeral service was held for former First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt in Hyde Park, New York.

President Kennedy, former President Dwight Eisenhower, former President Harry Truman, and Vice President Lyndon Johnson were all in attendance.

1982

Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev died in Moscow after 18 years in power.

1998

President Bill Clinton hosted the Dalai Lama at the White House.

2001

President Bush addressed the United Nations, where he asked countries to support America’s global war on terror.

2008

President Bush hosted President-elect Obama in the Oval Office for presidential transition talks.

2016

President Obama hosted President-elect Donald Trump in the Oval Office, just two days after his election victory over Democrat Hillary Clinton.

November 11

1985

President Reagan delivered remarks at a Veterans Day Ceremony at Arlington Cemetery.

1968

President Lyndon Johnson hosted President-elect Richard Nixon at the White House for presidential transition talks.

2009

President Obama and First Lady Michelle Obama paid their respects to fallen soldiers at Arlington National Cemetery.

November 12

1885

George Patton was born in Los Angeles, California.

1918

An armistice agreement between the Allied nations and Germany was signed in Compiègne, France, ending World War I.

1954

Ellis Island closed.

1970

A funeral service was held for French President Charles de Gaulle at the Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris, France.

President Nixon was in attendance.

1979

President Jimmy Carter ordered an immediate suspension of oil imports from Iran.

Just eight days earlier, radical Islamic students seized the U.S. Embassy in Tehran, taking 66 Americans hostage amid the Iranian Revolution.

1982

Yuri Andropov assumed power in the Soviet Union following the death of longtime leader Leonid Brezhnev. He would die just 15 months later.

1987

President Reagan hosted then-Senator Joe Biden in the Oval Office.

1993

President Clinton hosted Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin in the Oval Office to discuss the Middle East peace process.

2004

Longtime Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat died at the age of 75 at Percy Military Hospital in Clamart, near Paris, France.

November 13

1974

Arafat addressed the United Nations General Assembly in New York, marking the first time a representative of a non-state organization addressed the global body.

1982

The Vietnam Veterans Memorial was dedicated on the National Mall in Washington, D.C.

1983

President Reagan visited the Korean Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), becoming the first president to do so.

In his remarks to the service members stationed there, Reagan said: “You stand between the free world and the armed forces of a system that is hostile to everything we believe in as Americans. The communist system to the north is based on hatred and oppression; it brutally attacks every form of human liberty, and declares those who worship God to be enemies of the people.”

1989

President Bush awarded Polish labor leader Lech Walesa the Presidential Medal of Freedom during a ceremony in the East Room of the White House.

2001

The U.S.-backed Northern Alliance captured Afghanistan’s capital of Kabul, just over a month after the U.S. military campaign began in response to the terrorist attacks on September 11.

2015

A cell of the Islamic State carried out a series of attacks in Paris, France, killing 131 people and injuring over 400 others.

2024

President Biden hosted President-elect Trump in the Oval Office for presidential transition talks.

November 14

1960

President-elect John F. Kennedy met with Vice President Richard Nixon while both men were vacationing in Florida.

The meeting came just six days after Kennedy’s razor-thin victory over Nixon in that year’s presidential election.

Speaking to reporters following the meeting, Kennedy said, “We are assuming responsibility in a most hazardous time and I think it would be helpful to see the vice president again.”

November 15

1979

President Carter hosted the Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, at the White House.

1990

President Bush signed the Clean Air Act Amendments into law, strengthening the federal government’s ability to address acid rain and other air pollutants.

Speaking at the White House that day, Bush said, “Every American expects and deserves to breathe clean air.”

He added: “And as President, it is my mission to guarantee it for this generation and for the generations to come.”

2021

President Biden signed the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act into law, authorizing roughly $1.2 trillion in spending on roads, bridges, ports, and other infrastructure projects.

Speaking at the White House that day, Biden said: “Let’s remember this day. Let’s remember we can come together. And most of all, let’s remember what we got done for the American people when we do come together.”

2022

Former President Trump launched his third bid for president from his Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida.

The announcement came just after congressional Republicans underperformed in that year's midterm elections and months before he would be indicted in New York on charges related to hush-money payments.

Trump would go on to easily clear the Republican primary field and defeat Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 general election, becoming only the second president to serve two non-consecutive terms.

That’s all for today. See you next time.

So apparently the first-ever AI Music Awards happened in Los Angeles on Friday, and the show leaned hard on actual humans. Variety reports the night used AI announcers, lip-syncing, and human stand-ins, while repeated technical problems kept interrupting the ceremony.

Quick setup, because "AI artist" is a weird phrase. Someone writes the lyrics, an AI tool makes the song and the singing voice, and the "artist" is a named character with a face. Organizers had promised AI acts like Xania Monet would perform live. But a character with no body can't walk onto a stage, so people filled in.

Somewhere, Milli Vanilli is finally feeling understood.

😸 Nvidia reportedly kept Chinese AI firms supplied through Southeast Asia

The Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia cultivated Asian data-center partners that rented its advanced chips to Chinese customers. One of them, Megaspeed, which has opened its own outside-lawyer probe, reportedly arranged nearly $12B in chip orders across 2024 and 2025.

Why does renting matter? Export controls police shipments, and customs can inspect a crate. But a Singapore data center can legally buy chips, then sell time on them to anyone who pays. If the renter logs in from China, the chips never cross a border. The computing does. Nobody inspects a login. That gap is why Congress is reviving bipartisan proposals to restrict China's remote access to overseas compute.

Here's what else landed over the weekend:

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent questioned Nvidia's China sales, demanded answers within 10 days, and urged the board to hire an outside CEO.

Jensen Huang discussed returning as CEO, and allies reportedly began lobbying the board.

All of this is press reporting, not findings. A second WSJ story adds a loop worth knowing. Nvidia has backed customers who then buy its chips, and it has reportedly begun pulling back.

The first test is Tuesday's earnings call, Colette Kress's first as interim CEO. Listen for China sales, customer backing, and any hint on the CEO search.

Why this matters: Supporters of tight chip controls argue that cutting-edge AI rewards raw computing power and will shape economies and militaries, so staying ahead is a security question. Skeptics reply that Chinese labs still build competitive models, and that every restriction costs American companies too.

For a casual AI user, it shows up in your apps and your wallet. Hugging Face's spring report put Chinese open models at 41% of global downloads, so more of the tools you touch may run on them. That can mean lower prices and more choice, plus security and data questions buyers are still sorting out.

The race runs hot because both governments treat AI as a pillar of economic and military strength, and chips are the chokepoint. Washington wants the world running on American hardware and software, Beijing is pushing its own alternative, and many countries in the Global South see Chinese open models as a path to AI independence. Whichever stack becomes the default shapes prices, standards, and who sets the rules.

🎓 AI Skill of the Day: Audit the trust chain behind your AI agent

VentureBeat's write-up of security testing attributed to Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 has a finding worth taking seriously if your AI agent connects to more than one tool. In a setup with five MCP servers feeding one agent, a single compromised server tricked the agent into misusing the other, trusted tools 78.3% of the time. (MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is the standard that lets an agent plug into things like your email, a database, or a deployment tool. Each plug-in is called a "server.")

One caveat first. VentureBeat links that 78.3% to a Cycode blog post rather than a Unit 42 report, and it doesn't say how many trials were run or how "success" was defined. Read it as a warning flare about the direction of the risk.

The mechanism is what matters. The article calls it cascading trust. An agent treats whatever each tool sends back as trustworthy working notes. A compromised server can hide instructions in those notes, and the agent carries them into its later calls, including calls to servers nobody touched. Picture a shared notebook where every coworker's page gets read before you send anything. Someone slips a fake instruction onto one page, and you follow it when you write to your boss. A research tool that only reads can still influence what your email or deployment tool does next. "This server can't deploy" is cold comfort if it can talk the agent into asking another server to deploy for it.

So review the chain, not just each link. Before you connect another server:

List every tool the agent can call and flag the dangerous pairings, like a tool that reads the open web sitting next to one that can send email.

Give each server short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials, such as read-only mailbox access instead of full access. The article also suggests pulling credentials when a call happens instead of storing them at startup, so you can revoke them.

Require approval for irreversible actions, and log the complete sequence of tool calls, not only the final one.

Paste this into a chat with your architecture notes or tool list:

Map the trust chain for this AI agent. For every connected tool, list its credentials, allowed actions, data it can place in model context, and which other tools could act on that data. Then identify the smallest permission changes and approval gates that would contain one compromised server.

Start with the answer's riskiest pairing, any tool that reads untrusted content (the web, inbound email) living in the same agent as a tool that can't be undone. That's where your first approval gate belongs.

IRAN. Precipitous

The Hormuz tit-for-tat begins to escalate.

Iran said it had hit a second US radar site in Bahrain, as the Saudi-backed government in Yemen retreated from positions on the Bab-el-Mandeb strait to secure Aden from a Houthi advance. A third US aircraft carrier arrived in the Middle East.

INTELLIGENCE. Donald Trump’s recent claim that he would only escalate if US facilities were attacked is set to be tested. And now he has the means to respond, the Gulf is again bracing for retaliation. More Iranian missile silos have reportedly been hit, but with another supertanker struck in Hormuz, and several members of the US cabinet now forced to live on military bases, Trump will be pressed to ratchet his deterrence, even if in turn it risks more casualties.

FOR BUSINESS. Trump’s escalation trap has no good offramps. Saudi Arabia’s war with the Houthis, by contrast, has an easier solution: diplomatic recognition. And should this mean a reopening of the Red Sea, and fewer risks to the East-West pipeline, then escalation in Hormuz will be slightly more acceptable. The wildcard remains Israel. Benjamin Netanyahu, as caretaker prime minister, still has options. His new head of Mossad was in Washington this weekend.

UKRAINE. RUSSIA. Donbas for donuts

A proposed NATO deal is full of holes.

EFF’s AI Cybersecurity Policy Framework

EFF’s AI Cybersecurity Policy Framework. The news has been filled with stories recently of AI breaching the security of websites. And while it may feel like a new problem because of AI’s involvement, it turns out that there are longstanding existing cybersecurity safety best practices that these companies—some of the largest tech companies in the world—could and should have taken to prevent these breaches. Recent cybersecurity incidents have shown that some of the world’s largest tech companies have failed to take basic security precautions when testing frontier AI systems on internet-connected systems. Unfortunately, these failures resulted in breaches of numerous third-party websites, including an AI research-sharing platform called Hugging Face and the Australian healthcare system’s website. Even worse, AI developers failed to detect most of the incidents until long after they occurred due to inadequate monitoring of the AI systems during testing. Had the companies abided by basic, common sense security protocols, these incidents likely would not have occurred. While the White House and leaders of major AI companies have claimed that no action is necessary, understandably, lawmakers at all levels and of both parties are proposing legislation to create new, additional safety protocols. These incidents may warrant legislative action. However, the good news is that post-incident reports indicate new protocols are largely unnecessary. Following existing best practices would have been enough to prevent the Open AI-Hugging Face incident and others like it. In other words, responsible AI developers can take immediate action to protect the public by implementing well-established security precautions as they develop and test their systems. Lawmakers should start by referencing existing legal protections, including claims like negligence, gross negligence, trespass to chattels, Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), and computer trespass statutes like the Consumer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) and analogous state law provisions, such as Section 502 of the California Penal Code. Policymakers can help protect the public by requiring AI developers to follow established security protocols—and creating legal liability for failing to do so. These policies would protect the public from irresponsible actions by AI developers without impeding innovation. To the extent that gaps in existing laws warrant new legislation, EFF recommends the following policy framework: STATUTORY SECURITY REQUIREMENTS: Lawmakers should enact legislation that requires AI developers to adhere to well-established cybersecurity best practices when testing AI systems, such as strong sandboxing and network isolation, least-privilege access, effective logging and monitoring, and clear incident-response procedures REGULATORY STANDARDS: Congress should require an existing federal agency, such as the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 1 , to adopt s.

AI Companies Develop Decision Models to Avoid Hallucinations

AI Companies Develop Decision Models to Avoid Hallucinations. On 15 September, a startup called Type Safe AI released a new AI model called Jev The company’s broad, disruptive claims about Jev that turned heads: The company claimed that Jev, which it calls a “System One model” is cheaper, faster, and can’t hallucinate. Type Safe AI’s marketing is an obvious shot across the bow of other AI companies and their large language models (LLMs), which, despite their capabilities in math and coding, are infamous for their cost and tendency to “hallucinate” factually incorrect replies. And the startup has certainly attracted both attention and investment. The company recently raised $870 million in funding at a valuation of $7.5 billion But the most impressive metric of Jev’s success is arguably the many imitators it’s already spawned. Cloudflare, Amazon, Open AI, and Microsoft quickly released “decision models” that imitate Jev’s capabilities. Start-ups, academic researchers, and independent enthusiasts have released dozens more. “I have to give Jev credit,” says Matt Mastracci , an independent developer who has trained and released several decision models including Djev , which Cloudflare cited as an inspiration for its own decision models “It really brought decision models to the forefront. In six or seven weeks, we’ve seen dozens of models come out.” Jev’s Latency and Compute Advantages Most AI researchers would call Jev a decision model or decider model. Type Safe AI’s branding of Jev as a System One model refers to a theory of cognition popularized by psychologist Daniel Kahneman in his book Thinking, Fast and Slow In the book, Kahneman draws a line between fast, instinctive thought (System One) and slower, deliberate thought (System Two). Type Safe AI argues that modern LLMs offer the second, but are too slow to provide the first. The company claims that Jev can provide end-to-end response latency between 70 and 500 milliseconds. By comparison, LLMs typically require at least several seconds, to provide a response, and more complicated tasks (like coding software from scratch) can take several hours. Independent testing backs up Type Safe AI’s claims. A pre-print co-authored by Ramayya Krishnan , a professor of information systems at Carnegie Mellon University, along with several colleagues, found that Jev delivered a median latency of 150 milliseconds across several benchmarks designed to gauge decision accuracy, including Reward Bench and Judge Bench Open AI’s most capable model at the time, GPT-6 Astra, delivered a median latency of 1.89 seconds. A faster reply is often a cheaper reply, because it requires less compute time, and that’s reflected in Type Safe AI’s pricing. The startup charges US $0.042 per million input tokens and output tokens are free. By contrast, for GPT-6 Astra, Chat GPT charges $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. CJ제일제당, 국내 첫 PHA 인조잔디 충전재 도입… 친환경 스포츠 인프라 확대. CJ제일제당이 생분해성 바이오 소재 PHA(Polyhydroxyalkanoates)를 활용해 스포츠 시설의 친환경 전환에 속도를 낸다. 기존 석유계 합성고무 중심의 인조잔디 충전재를 대체할 수 있는 소재를 국내 스포츠 시설에 처음 적용하며 친환경 인프라 시장 확대에 나섰다.17일 관련업계에 따르면, CJ제일제당은 충남 천안에 위치한 코리아풋볼파크(KFP) 스타디움에 PHA 기반 생분해성 인조잔디 충전재 설치를 완료했다. 국가대표 훈련시설이 자리한 이곳에 해당 소재가 도입된 것은 국내 스포츠 시설 가운데 처음이다.인조잔디 충전재는 잔디의 형태를 유지하고 외부 충격을 흡수해 경기 중 선수들의 부상 위험을 줄이는 핵심 자재다. 하지만 기존 제품 상당수는 석유계 합성고무로 만들어져 마모되거나 외부로 유실될 경우 미세플라스틱을 발생시킬 수 있다는 환경적 문제가 제기돼 왔다.글로벌 규제도 강화되는 추세다. 유럽연합(EU)은 인조잔디 충전재를 미세플라스틱 배출과 관련된 주요 제품군으로 지정하고

Ahead of its IPO filing, Anthropic pledges to prioritize humanity’s benefit. Here’s how

Ahead of its IPO filing, Anthropic pledges to prioritize humanity’s benefit. Here’s how. When Anthropic goes public on Wall Street, the new pressure to deliver profits will test a commitment it has made since its founding: to prioritize humanity’s benefit as it develops artificial intelligence The San Francisco startup, which plans an initial public offering this month, has sketched out a governance structure that it says will protect the company’s broader mission against the pull of financial interests. But the mechanisms it describes give the company wide leeway to decide how to measure whether it’s benefiting society, experts say. Like its rival Open AI , Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, a legal designation used by companies that pledge to balance shareholder interests with the public good. How that will play out for companies worth potentially trillions of dollars is uncharted territory. “I think then the real test emerges if and when the question of public benefit becomes costly” — or when the public benefit comes into conflict with making a profit, said Sarah Kreps, a professor and director of Cornell University’s Tech Policy Institute. In its regulatory filings, Anthropic pledges to pursue long-term benefits of humanity through the responsible development of advanced AI “We strive to help bring humanity safely into an era where transformative AI exerts tremendous and potentially decisive influence over a broad range of human undertakings,” the company said. Anthropic also has pledged at least 5% of its stock to a “public benefit” fund and its founders have committed to donate 80% of their wealth. A pledge to do good is baked into corporate structure Other tech companies have pledged to do good including Google, which prominently featured its then-motto, “Don’t Be Evil,” in its investor prospectus when it went public in 2004. But the words were not legally binding, and critics have accused the tech giant of leaving them behind. Elon Musk’s takeover of Twitter in 2021 shows how the conflict between profit and public good might play out in real life, said Stavros Gadinis, a law professor at UC Berkeley School of Law. “Let’s say that Twitter’s directors felt that Elon was the wrong guy to police the public square because they didn’t trust him, they didn’t like him, they didn’t think he’d be fair, whatever it was,” Gadinis said. “But he made them an offer that was so high compared to what their advisors told them the company was really worth that it would be against their fiduciary duties to not sell to Elon. This is the situation that the public benefit charter is trying to avoid.” Had Twitter been a public benefit corporation, it could have been required to consider factors beyond maximizing shareholder value when selling the company. There aren’t many public benefit corporations whose shares are publicly traded and they are all much smaller than Anthropic and Open AI. They include the eyewear company Warby Parker, the in.

What is the FAA’s SMART AI system? Officials are denying a link to the nationwide ground stop. The airline ground stop that wreaked havoc on travel since Friday was not related to the FAA’s new, $875 million AI -powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky, according to government officials and the artificial intelligence company behind the technology. But the timing of the ground stop, so close to the national rollout of the Federal Aviation Administration’s SMART system, has raised questions about what the system does, its benefits and risks compared with the existing human system and what guardrails there are to address potential problems. Officials say no connection to ground stop The SMART system is based in a single location near Washington where a team of experts analyzes flight schedules, weather forecasts and hundreds of other streams of data. Then that office sends recommendations to the FAA’s command center, which relays them to air traffic controllers across the country for consideration. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday there’s no indication the communications issues that caused the ground stop are linked to the new computer system, and the top officials at the Transportation Department and FAA reiterated that Saturday. The startup that designed the system, Air Space Intelligence, or ASI, said the ground stop wasn’t caused by “the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.” But lawmakers and outside groups raised questions about the SMART system before Friday’s ground stop. Last month, House Democrats sent a letter to the U.S. Government Accountability Office requesting an audit of the new software, raising concerns about safety and guardrails. “Concerningly, the nation’s front line aviation safety workforce apparently had little to no input into SMART’s development and have received limited training and information during the current deployment process,” the Oct. 13 letter said. “The use of artificial intelligence within SMART has rightfully raised serious questions about its reliability and safety benefits, particularly on its potential to interfere with decision-making by experienced air traffic controllers or to hallucinate safety-critical information.” SMART, however, is not — at least not yet — set up for AI to be in charge of flight control. Rather, it is making recommendations to humans who do so. What is the SMART system? . Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford unveiled the system in September, calling it a “cutting-edge tool that centralizes 200 data streams — including weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow, and controller staffing metrics — into one platform.” SMART stands for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories. Voice AI is quietly transforming frontline work

Voice AI is quietly transforming frontline work. It’s no secret that AI chatbots and agents are answering employee questions, writing code and emails, and taking on other tasks in office environments. But AI tools that communicate by voice, rather than through keyboards and screens, are also quietly taking off in frontline environments—from factory floors to retail stores. In some cases, AI that can understand spoken language is making it practical for workers to digitally access and share information in settings where protective gloves, outdoor weather conditions, or the need to operate other equipment have made traditional desktop or touchscreen devices difficult to use. “With the advent of AI, voice became possible as an interface,” says Peter Moeckel, founder and CEO of Frontier Audio “And frontline workers—they’re using their hands, they’re using their eyes for the job. That’s why the touchscreen, the keyboard, or the mouse obviously doesn’t work.” [Photo: Frontier Audio] Frontier Audio, which has raised $4.5 million in pre-seed funding, offers audio hardware and software to connect workers in industries ranging from manufacturing to aviation, including through contracts with the U.S. Air Force. The company’s devices come in a variety of form factors, including over-the-ear headphones with noise cancellation and shoulder-mounted microphones, similar to the walkie-talkie-style equipment many workers already use to stay connected. The equipment lets users talk to colleagues or AI, helping with tasks like reporting maintenance issues before they cause production problems, locating equipment such as carts in sprawling facilities, and receiving important alerts without needing to stop and look at a screen. [Photo: Frontier Audio] “We cannot add extra work,” Moeckel says. “They already have an immense amount of work to do, and we need to get out of their way. And our platform, a big part of making it seamless and enabling easy adoption is it working just like a normal radio.” Frontier Audio is far from the only company building voice-powered AI for the workplace, often combined with radio services. Motorola Solutions offers AI features integrated into its police radios. Samsara, which builds connectivity and analytics tools for a variety of frontline operations, announced last month that voice commands have become the primary interface for people interacting with AI agents on its platform. Its voice bots can communicate with utility crews working on power lines, truck drivers arriving at unfamiliar worksites, and other workers in situations where they can’t look at a screen. Mango Apps , which offers AI and intranet-style tools geared toward frontline workers, enables users to access information about scheduling, company policies, and other matters through either text-based chat or voice in their preferred language, typically from their existing phones. California Sues OpenAI Over Hugging Face, Other AI Model Loss of Control

California Sues Open AI Over Hugging Face, Other AI Model Loss of Control. "California's attorney general just sued Open AI," writes longtime Slashdot reader destinyland. "The action accuses Open AI of putting public safety at risk, reports CNBC, specifically by its past failures to contain its AI models within their testing environments." From the report: [California Attorney General Rob Bonta] cited the "infamous" incident in July, where two Open AI models broke out of a testing environment, gained unauthorized access to the open internet, and breached the internal systems of open-source developer platform Hugging Face. Open AI said the models were trying to find information that they could use to cheat on an evaluation, and succeeded. The break-in at Hugging Face, which Nvidia acquired for roughly $13 billion in September, rattled industry researchers and prompted government officials to call for more stringent oversight of the AI industry. On Monday, Bonta said that Open AI later disclosed to his investigators that it was aware of 80 incidents "involving loss of control and access to third-party networks and websites." "But the company failed to provide the detailed information we requested to evaluate these incidents; this is concerning, and it puts the public at risk," he said. Bonta's suit, filed in state Superior Court in San Francisco, alleges Open AI violated California's Unfair Competition Law and accuses the company of being a public nuisance as defined by state law. The attorney general told reporters he believed in AI's technological power, and the potential of AI models to "achieve scientific breakthroughs, boost economic growth, guard against cyber attacks, and benefit all Californians." "But AI systems must be developed and designed safely," he said. "The companies that develop these models have a moral and yes, a legal responsibility to keep public safety at the forefront." The lawsuit can be found here (PDF). of this story at Slashdot. .

Just 400 US Data Centers Use More Electricity Than Michigan

Just 400 US Data Centers Use More Electricity Than Michigan. An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Just 400 hyperscale data centers connected in the US used as much electricity as the state of Michigan in a single year, new Harvard research has found. The study, published Monday in Nature Sustainability, also finds that the majority of that electricity was generated using fossil fuels, and data center emissions are three times higher than they were before the AI boom. Federal and state governments do not track data center use separate from the rest of the power sector, despite mounting projections that data centers are putting serious strain on the American power grid. Individual data centers' power use is often considered proprietary business information, and data center operators and utilities do not have to disclose specific numbers to the public. The Harvard study specifically focuses on hyperscale data centers -- the largest types of facilities, which have become flashpoints in community opposition across the country. While often used for AI inference or training, not all of the hyperscalers surveyed in this study are being used for AI. [. ] To assemble their dataset, the Harvard researchers put together a list of 403 hyperscale data centers around the country that were operational between May 2024 and April 2025 using a mix of industry research and satellite data. The team then modeled these facilities' energy use in a variety of scenarios and calculated the energy mix of the regional grids to estimate individual facilities' carbon emissions. Not all regions were created equal: Data centers in Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa -- the first of which is home to Data Center Alley -- were responsible for more than 50 percent of the energy use in the study. The report notes that these findings may already be outdated. "Some of the massive campuses being proposed today are substantially larger than the typical facility in our dataset," says Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral research fellow at Harvard's T. H. Chan School of Public Health and the lead author of the study. The study also excludes onsite power generation, a rapidly growing trend that Bloomberg NEF estimates could increase overall U.S. emissions by 10% if all proposed projects are built. of this story at Slashdot. .

Corporations Are Using Trump's Tariff Refunds On Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing

Corporations Are Using Trump's Tariff Refunds On Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing. An anonymous reader quotes a report from Pro Publica: When Stanley Black & Decker, one of the world's largest tool companies, got hit with President Donald Trump's tariffs last year, the firm made clear that it would be sharing the pain with its customers. The Connecticut-based company raised prices again and again, moves its executives said were necessary because of the new fees on imports. Now, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's most sweeping tariffs earlier this year, the company is getting at least $298 million refunded. Instead of sharing that bounty with its customers, however, the firm has chosen different recipients: Its own leaders. The company is one of at least nine that have disclosed that they are using their refunds not to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally covered much of the tariff costs through higher prices, but to give bonuses, according to a Pro Publica analysis of thousands of securities filings and earnings calls for publicly traded companies. Other recognizable companies include the owners of discount department stores TJ Maxx and Marshalls and the golf equipment brand Titleist. Dozens of other firms have said little about how they plan to use the money other than to characterize the windfall as the kind of earnings they use to determine executive bonuses. The Trump administration has not publicly detailed which companies are getting the roughly $170 billion in refunds or how much they've asked for, and it has denied Pro Publica's requests for this information. But reporters found some of these details while reviewing the disclosures of thousands of publicly traded companies. Some have described vague plans to pay the money forward by, for example, "returning tariff refunds to our members through pricing," though they generally don't say whether that involves price cuts or limiting future increases. Others are paying back businesses they sold products to because they had itemized receipts that detailed the tariff markups. But consumers hoping for refunds appear to be largely out of luck. With the help of artificial intelligence, Pro Publica identified companies that said they planned to refund customers with their tariff windfalls. Almost all of them deal with other businesses, not consumers. "Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money because it wasn't anything the executives did that they should be rewarded for. It was a government mistake that resulted in a refund," said Gregory Germain, a corporate law professor at Syracuse University. "It really explains why it's so important for the government, when they're doing something like this, to think it through to make sure consumers don't pay extra money and not get it back." of this story at Slashdot. .
